subtopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, June 10, consideration of the motion of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Minister of Finance)
^Mr- Guthrie.]
that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the forty minute limit accorded to private members is so short as to render it impossible for me to deal with all the various subjects covered by the budget. Therefore I shall have to omit all matters with which it will be possible to deal at some future time. Unfortunately two I shall have to omit are of great importance to the constituency I represent. The first one concerns the question of unemployment. I will crystallize my observations in that connection into one sentence. I have had several occasions to speak concerning this subject, and at this time I would simply say without collusion with any other hon. member of the house, that I believe it is the duty of the official opposition and the independent groups in this corner of the chamber, together with private members on the government side of the house, if they have any regard for the interests of their constituents, to exercise the only power they have by refusing to vote supply until the government of the day has brought down a statement of the policy they propose to pursue to deal not only with the immediate distress confronting us but also with the .situation which we will have next winter. We should secure also an assurance that they will bring down a measure-as bring it down they must-providing money for such relief at a time sufficiently previous to the close of the session that hon. members may be in a position to discuss the measure in a fair and proper manner. The practice is played out of bringing down a measure only about twenty-four hours before the close of the session and threatening that if the money is not quickly voted the measure will not be passed. That plan worked all right in the short session but it will not be accepted a second time.
The next matter I had intended to discuss was that of coal which in my district is a most important one. Unfortunately the facts in connection with this commodity are too lengthy to deal with to-day, but I will have an opportunity at a later time. I pledged myself both publicly and privately to vote for the budget, no matter what it contained, if it contained a measure in relief of our coal industry, so desperate are conditions. I do not mean to say I made a deal with the government or any member of it but I merely made a voluntary statement to that effect. The question now before me is: Must I, or

The Budget-Mr. Neill
should I, vote for this budget? True, we have received a measure of assistance, if that can be called assistance which with one hand gives a dollar and with the other takes away ninety-nine cents, or to 'be exact 98.3 cents. I wish I had time to go more fully into the matter of coal. I would' like to say however that the government have produced and laid down in their budget the frame work of a national fuel policy which will be quite satisfactory to many parts of Canada and would be satisfactory to us, if we were put in line with the said policy. The fact is, however, that we have not been. To illustrate briefly, may I say that Nova Scotia under the terms of the fuel policy may get assistance to the extent of S2.25 per ton whereas we can get only 1.7 cents per ton. I do not wish to be misunderstood by the press and repeat that I am not stating the figure to be $1.07, but one cent and seven-tenths of a cent per ton. We asked for $1.50 and probably would have been satisfied with $1.25 so that we would have been in a position to get into the South American market. I ask hon. members how far will 1.7 cents take us into that market.
I feel almost inclined to vote for the budget for one reason, namely, that it will afford no opportunity for an alibi and no excuse to say, "Well, we brought down the framework and if the hon. member for Comox-Alberni had done his share and voted for it we would in committee have adjusted any details." That statement would be too absolutely absurd on the face of it. I can point to the situation in the adjoining constituency of Nanaimo, represented by an hon. member who is well known to be a very staunch supporter of the party in power (Mr. Dickie), where a condition exists very similar to that existing in the district I have the honour to represent. I think the policy of the government will affect my hon. friend's constituents worse if anything than it will affect mine. I know the Prime Minister has received during the last few days a great many telegrams and without further comment I shall leave the question of coal in the hope that he will meet faith with faith and put us on a par-we do not ask anything else; we dio not ask for privileges or preferences-but so far as the fuel policy is concerned to put us on a par with the other sections of Canada. I think I am not asking too much.
Now I come to the budget. The budget reveals an enormous deficit for which I do not blame the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When my hon. friend
refers to par does he mean %o of a cent per ton mile from the seaboard?

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I do not refer to the
same rate per mile, but that we should be given the same consideration by way of more bonus. For instance, on a percentage basis, the total cost is reckoned at $1,800,000. We would be entitled to or about $257,000 or $258,000. As a matter of fact we get only $20,000. A policy which will enable us to do the thing advocated by the government, that is, which will let us get into the foreign market, by granting $2.25 to Nova Scotia, $2 to Alberta and-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, not foreign markets, but quite the opposite.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, what is the difference?
What is the use of quibbling about a word. We want a market, and in our case we have to take a foreign market. In Alberta they have the opportunity of trading in a Canadian market. I should suppose we would be more entitled to a preference in order to get into a foreign market than to get into a domestic market. The object of the change is undoubtely to open a market. Alberta and Nova Scotia are amply provided for, but in the province of British Columbia the matter is a jest, not even a gesture.
Concerning the budget I have already said there is an enormous deficit. Certainly I cannot blame the Prime Minister for that. There is an enormous increase in taxation and for that I do not blame him. He has stated that the unsatisfactory condition is due to world-wide causes; certainly that is true, and I agree with him. I told my electors that and also told them that the Mackenzie King government was not responsible for the worldwide depression. Unfortunately the right hon. the Prime Minister placed himself in a false position when he did not tell the same thing to the electors. He told them that the fault could be traced to the Mackenzie King government and that if he were placed in power a cure would be effected. "Not a man idle in 1931" was the rallying cry in my constituency. "This I will do." Unfortunately that statement has now to be translated in the terms, "This I cannot do unless you give me unlimited time." I wonder if those people who elected Moses to lead the children of Israel out of Egypt into the Promised Land would have been so unanimous in their choice had it been known that they were to spend forty years in the wilderness, and that every adult would die and none of them would enter the Promised Land. I wonder if the electors of Canada had been similarly informed what the result would have been. Of course, I admit frankly, and any reasonable
The Budget-Mr. Neill

man must, that times will improve. In time, with the turning of the wheel, the cycle, inevitably, conditions will be improved. I would be quite willing to guarantee that. However, for the moment I am going to accept the argument put forward by the right hon. Prime Minister. He says the conditions are world-wide; I grant that. He says they are not due to the late government or to his own government; I grant even that, although there is some suggestion that as conditions have gotten worse since the new government took office it is to some extent responsible. But I will go the whole length and say, yes, he is blameless. But you must allow me this logical sequence: At the next election when conditions must inevitably be better than they are now, it will not be in order for him to take credit for the change and say that it is the result of his policies. I want it to be written in capital letters in Hansard: The understanding is that he is not responsible for bad times now, and consequently he will not be responsible for the improved conditions when they come.
I propose to deal very briefly with some of the items of increased taxation, which I am afraid will be open to very much criticism. There will be a great deal of dissatisfaction with that portion of the budget which substantially cuts down the income tax of the rich man. My hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) in a very admirable speech estimated that 80 per cent of the increased taxation will be paid by the man of small means. I hope it will not be as bad as that, but it will be substantially so. I am thinking of the man of small income where the woman of the house is the chancellor of the exchequer. She gets her husband's salary week by week, or month by month, and she is going to get a horrible shock when she next tries to budget her husband's week's wages or month's salary. She is going to run up against the heavily increased sales tax, she is going to find a substantial increase in the tax on tea, and a very heavy increase in the tax on rice-I do not know why. She will also find that there is a very heavy increase in the tax on raisins and oranges, amounting in the aggregate, it is claimed, to $4,000,000 on oranges. I do not know as to that. It is said that oranges are a luxury and need not be eaten by poor people. I would remind hon. members that oranges are no longer a luxury; doctors prescribe them very freely and they enter very considerably into the diet of babies and young children. I presume raisins and oranges are taxed to enable 
us to dicker with the Australian government in negotiating the new treaty that we have heard a good deal about. If so, I sincerely hope that there will be a provision inserted in the budget that if the negotiations for the treaty fail, these heavy taxes will cease to be effective.
The farmer who deals nowadays largely with cooperative concerns is going to be severely hit by the cheque tax, and also by the heavier postage rate. As the right hon. gentleman says, the man who issues the cheque pays the tax, but I fear the farmer will find it deducted from his monthly cheque. The tax has been substantially increased on vegetable and farm seeds, just at the time of the year when money is hard to obtain.
In regard to the poultryman, I thought he had reached hell's deepest hell, but it appears that the government of the day has discovered a still deeper level-a sort of basement. They have put a duty on corn, which means that the man raising chickens will have to pay $2.90 instead of $2 for a sack of corn-probably by the time the duty is pyramided the sack will cost him $3, or 50 per cent of a tax. Now we are told, "You must use barley." It would be about as reasonable to say, "We will encourage the sale of pyjamas by putting a heavy tax on nightshirts." Then the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) said that we ought to feed the hens barley instead of corn. The trouble with the hon. gentleman is that he never was a hen, and does not know the hen psychology. Unfortunately the hen is not open to tariff considerations. There are three things you cannot fool in this world so far as I know: You cannot fool with Mother Earth-if you don't feed her she won't respond; you cannot fool a milking cow; you cannot fool a laying hen.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about chickens?

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My experience with chickens of the type my hon. friend refers to is somewhat ancient, but in my young and salad days I remember associating with them under conditions when I learned a good deal of their reaction to foods and particularly expensive foods, also generally connected with a cover charge of about $9. The loveliest chicken but excuse me, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I have time to go into the subject any further, especially with my wife in the gallery.
Now I come to an item in the budget to which considerable space and time were given,

The Budget-Mr. Neill
that dealing with the 87 concerns that have allegedly come into this country by reason of the budget changes last September. It is good propaganda of its class, it is a statement that may easily be carried around. It will be discussed at tea tables and in stores and in beer parlours, and it will be easy to say, "It is perfectly true because I saw it all in print." The trouble is you cannot believe all that appears in print. Let me quote a few words of the right hon. Prime Minister, who was cautious in his reference:
It will be some time before full details in regard to capital invested, number employed, etc., can be secured since some are still in process of organization,-
Truer words were never written. I wonder how many of those concerns are in that condition. I notice a good many of them are not even incorporated. My hon. friend who sits next to me and myself can go down the street, hire an office and put up a sign: "Company for the Extraction of Gold from Sea Water." We do not need to have any capital or any gold, we do not even need to have any sea water. All we need do is call ourselves a company and we will be eligible to enter into this select circle. Don't you think, Mr. Speaker, that before we accept these 87 concerns we should know whether they were operating and how many men they were employing-and if they are employing men I would want to know why the unemployment figures are going up instead of down. Don't you think, sir, that the usual fluctuation of business has something to do with it? I have a record somewhere that I took out of the Gazette where it says that three substantial companies, one of them nationally known, were giving up their charters in Canada and going out of business. Look at the Gazette and you see on one page the number of companies that have become bankrupt or disincorporated and on the next page the number of companies incorporated and starting up in business. It is simply one against the other. It would be as reasonable to claim credit for the number of births since the introduction of last session's tariffs without taking into account the number of deaths. Indeed, no credit could be claimed even then for a high tariff means a low birth-rate. It is a well-known fact in Britain that the price of bread has a direct relation to the number of marriages. I may say that since I saw this budget I have determined not to have any more of a family; I simply cannot afford it.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about hens?

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am past hens. I notice that in the list no less than three out of the eighty-seven concerns there named are pencil companies. Our imports of pencils are very small. There was no increased tariff on pencils during the special session. Therefore these three companies are not going into the business on account of the benefits offered them last September. Why they are starting operations is best known to themselves, but certainly that is not the reason. I see in this budget they are to get an increase to 35 per cent instead of 27J per cent. Surely it will not be asserted that they knew beforehand what the budget was going to contain I If in the last eight months those three companies thought it wise to start up on such a small output as is represented by the imports, why is it necessary to give any more tariff protection? Tariff protection is supposed to be necessary to help a new and struggling industry.
Then I find in the list, the Hump Hairpin Company-not limited. We will suppose it deals primarily with hairpins; that is reasonable. We do not expect to find them dealing in cement or coal, any more than we would expect to find a coal company dealing in watches. This company does not even deal in celluloid combs, which are much used by ladies nowadays; these hairpins are made of iron, because they are mentioned in that category in the budget. The imports are very small; they are not segregated, but as far as I can make out a fair estimate of the value of the imports of hairpins during last year would be some $42,000. There was no change of tariff during the short session, so this is not a case of a company being established through the tariff proposals of last year. I do not know anything about the Hump Hairpin Company; I have not had time to investigate them, but I venture to predict that the basement of the plant will not be dug before they will be here howling for more protection. They will not be able to put up the tariff very much higher, so it is reasonable to suppose they will ask -the government to compel the ladies to give up bobbing their hair, so that they will be compelled to use more hairpins. I want to say to the leader of the government that this absolutely will not do. It is all very well to talk about blasting a way here and there; he may get away with it for a time here or at the Imperial conference, but as there is a heaven above us, if he interferes with those people who bob their hair, he is headed for trouble. It may be all very well to interfere with men, but do not dare interfere with the ladies or
The Budget-Mr. Neill

they will bury the Prime Minister under a pile of his unwanted hairpins.
Of these 87 alleged cases of manufacturers coming to Canada, I find by the most casual, trival inspection that five per cent have not gone into business on account of the increased tariff. How many more there are, only time will show. Nearly every hon. member who gets up on this side of the house punctures one of these toy balloons in his particular district. Might I ask why we should encourage the foreigner to come and why we should not encourage Canadians to start in business? If I began an industry I would have a disposition to buy Canadian machinery and to employ Canadian workmen, but my name would not be embalmed for all time in the records of the government of Canada. These foreigners, however, who have established plants in Canada, are to be given a place of honour. Would it not be better to encourage Canadian capital to develop these industries?	,
I notice in this list only one plant located west of Ontario. That is what I warned my electors against; I told them the last campaign was to be a battle between the eastern manufacturers and the primary producers of the west. What have the farmers, the fishermen, the lumbermen and the coal men been given by the budget? I have already mentioned the blow to the poultrymen. The farmers have been given another body blow, little as they deserve it, in connection with the five cent bonus on wheat, which only applies to wheat for export and not for domestic use. The result will be this: The associated cooperative pools of British Columbia will send a man to Calgary, let us say, to buy six or seven carloads of wheat. He will make a deal at a fixed price f.o.b. Vancouver, say of 70 cents per bushel, and everything will be lovely. However, when he turns to leave the vendor will say, "I suppose you are going to export this wheat? The buyer will say, "No, I am not." Then the other man will say, "I am sorry but you will have to pay an extra five cents per bushel, because if I exported the wheat I would get five cents per bushel from the government." Under the previous discrimination-I might almost say infernal discrimination-between domestic and export freight rates we demonstrated that we could ship export wheat to China and pay sixty cents of the rate back for the same rate for which we could ship wheat to British Columbia, but this will be worse; it will be $1.65 per ton more. We will be able to ship export wheat to China and all the way back to Vancouver for the rate on domestic wheat.

That is 6,000 miles. Since then I have seen in the home papers-and although it is perhaps an unpatriotic thing to say, I wish them more power-that it is proposed to form a combination of buyers of wheat in British Columbia and send seven thousand miles away to Australia, of all places, for wheat. It is alleged that if they take a whole ship load they will be able to lay it down in British Columbia for less than they can buy it in Alberta, where they are burning grain for fuel. A government which makes conditions under which things of this kind are possible will be the laughing stock of the British Empire. Let me revert to a suggestion I made previously. I have personal reasons for being anxious to finish this session as quickly as possible, but I am willing to join the British Columbia members in refusing to vote supply until this gross injustice, which cannot be defended by any logic, is remedied.
Now we come to the fishing industry. Last session the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) and myself begged the government not to put a higher tax on gasoline used by fishermen; we asked them to follow the example of the provinces, which gave a rebate. However, they put on this tax, and they also put on the dumping duty which is fixed by the minister. He fixes anything he likes. The other day his department refused to accept the well known fact of the low prices of gasoline in the United States, and the reason given was that these prices were due to a rate war. How did the minister know it was a rate war? The price was universal and we were entitled to the advantage of that low price in the United States, but he said it was a rate war. Where he got that idea I do not know, but it resulted in a heavy dumping duty being applied. I know of one enthusiastic official who not only put on the dumping duty, which he was not entitled to do, but tried to go back six months and collect something like $300. I have here a wire from a fisherman, which I will just summarize. He says they are getting nine cents for their fish in Seattle, the only market for that class of fish. There is a duty of two cents, and freight and brokerage amounts to four cents, and he says he can buy gasoline in Seattle for 8 cents per imperial gallon, while at home he has to pay 26 cents per gallon. Remember, these men are competing in the same extraterritorial waters with American fishermen, who do not have to pay the two cents duty on the fish brought to Seattle, and who have the advantage of this cheap gasoline. This fisherman says they cannot keep it up, that

The Budget-Mr. Neill
operations will have to be discontinued unless the dumping duty is lifted. In addition, the United States government, probably the state government, in an attempt to do what was fair and just has recently agreed to take off a five cent tax in order to help the fishermen. I think our government might do the same thing, but will they do so? Here is another item from a local paper.
Spring salmon gill-netters on the Skeena river have suspended operations, because it is impossible to meet expenses on five cents per pound straight basis.
And with the price of gasoline 26 cents per gallon. This is what we are suffering from. I should have liked to say something more on this subject, but I must hurry on. This is crippling the fisherman who has his own little boat and who makes his living in that way. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, it will be quite all right when the spell-binders of our friends opposite go around and tell the fisherman that on the first $10,000 of his income he will not have to pay income tax if derived from dividends. Once he gets that fixed in his mind of course everything will be all right.
The government, with their policy, have lost the New Zealand preference for our salmon. That will cost us $65,000 this year, on the basis of last year, because the New Zealand government has cancelled the British preference so far as we are concerned. It may be said, and I admit, that I voted with the present government, then in opposition, in favour of doing away with the New Zealand agreement with regard to butter, and the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, did cancel that agreement and put on a tax of four cents per pound. New Zealand was quite satisfied, because they were conscious that they had been getting rather the best of the bargain. The National Dairy Council, who are accused by some of my Liberal friends of being Tories, warned the government not to go beyond four cents per pound. This government put on a duty of eight cents per pound, and it is that which has cost us in British Columbia our New Zealand market and our preference of $1.25 per case. Now the prime minister of New Zealand says they had to take this action because there was no hope of further negotiations. I want to tell you this, Mr. Speaker: the government of the day will have to keep these fishermen next winter; there is no other way out of it. They did not get any relief last winter; they struggled through as best they could. They will have to get some relief this year.
The lumber and paper industry will be largely dependent on the terms of the Australian treaty. I will not say anything in that regard that might hamper the minister in his negotiations. Until we get the treaty we cannot know what the terms are. I hope our fish, lumber and pulp interests will be taken care of.
I wish now to discuss old age pensions, but there is another matter I should like to speak on and I may have to sacrifice that question. However, in case I am called off in the middle of a syllable by the turning-over of the official hour-glass, I wish to summarize the things which we in my district want. We want the coal bonus increased in line with the aid given to other portions of Canada-only justice, and not any favours or anything of that sort. We want the farmers protected against any further handicap by the discrimination against the domestic rate in regard to the 5 cents bonus. We want the unemployment policy brought down. And we want the matter I am.going to speak of now, attended to-that is, in regard to pilchards.
The matter of pilchards is a long story. Pilchards are a species of herring and the industry is entirely confined to the west coast of Vancouver island, where they reduce the fish into oil and meal. At one time there were twenty-seven expensive plants operating on that coast whereas to-day there are possibly only six, most of which have either gone bust or are shut down. Now, the people engaged in this industry asked the government to put a duty on raw vegetable oil brought in for the manufacture of domestic shortening. Cocoanut and palm oils, etc,, are brought in from the United States, and the people whom I represent want a duty imposed to check the importation of these oils. These oils are used in the manufacture of shortening such as Crisco and so forth, and if a duty were imposed it would curtail the importation of these oils and encourage the use of pilchard oil. At one time this oil sold at 50 cents a gallon; now it is 15 cents a gallon with a duty of 5 cents a gallon going into the United States. Almost the only market now is in the United States, where it is used for the very purpose for which we in Canada are not allowed to use it. There is another aspect to this matter. In addition to the request for the duty on vegetable oils, we are asking that we be allowed in Canada to sell shortening made with pilchard oil instead of from palm oil or cocoanut oil, and that we be allowed to describe it as an article made with edible oil. This is what is done in the United States. But the officials in some department here have so far refused this permission. I am not blaming this government; the same atti-
The Budget-Mr. Neill

tude was taken under the former administration. The fact is, however, that some moss-backed official said, "No; the traditions of the past are good enough for me and mine." It has always been considered that oil produced from fish must develop a rancid odour and be objectionable and therefore any shortening made from such oil must be branded "Made with fish oil," and that damns the whole thing; the housewife will not buy it. But, Mr. Speaker, time Moves. It does not appear to move with the officials here but it moves in the United States; for in that country they have discovered a process known as hydrogenation, oy which, at large expense, with a plant costing a million and a half, they have entirely removed the possibility of pilchard oil becoming rancid or having any disagreeable odour. The result is that in the United States the manufacturers are permitted by the government to use this oil for this particular purpose. And surely they are. just as punctilious in the United States as we are in regard to the purity of foodstuffs. There the manufacturers are allowed to sell shortening made from this oil under the description "Made with edible oils," and that very product is brought into and sold in Canada. We buy it here; yet we are not allowed to use the same oil, produced in Canada, for the same purpose, notwithstanding that this would build up a prosperous business in this country and give employment to our fishermen. We cannot do this because someone in the department thinks that the product ought to be marked "Made from fish oil." This attitude taken by the officials has resulted in two thousand men being out of employment, men who are in dire need of work. These companies have wired the Prime Minister, and I have a telegram from them to the same effect. If their request were granted it would make a tremendous difference and would provide work for two thousand men. And there is no reason in the world why this should not be done except that someone declares that inasmuch as it has always been regarded as objectionable to have fish oil used in this way, it must necessarily continue for all tame to be objectionable, notwithstanding that, as I have pointed out, the reason for the objection has been entirely removed. It has been absolutely demonstrated; samples have been submitted to the government analysts, and they have agreed that there is nothing objectionable in the oil. But the departmental officials will not allow the product to be sold under the label "Made with edible oils." At the same time, however, they will allow any stuff to come in from the South Pacific islands 
because it is represented as a vegetable oil product. I trust the government will see its way to meet the request of these companies in this matter. All the Prime Minister need do is wave his hand, and it will be done. It will not involve any question of protection, it will cost no one anything, simply to have the article designated properly. I am informed that a company is willing to put up money and build a hydrogenation .plant right away in Canada, and this would be a splendid thing indeed for the fishing industry. There is hardly anything I can think of that would be better just now for the industry.
I should like to say a word or two in connection with old age pensions. We were told that the maritime provinces could not give their aged people pensions unless this government contributed 100 per cent, and the present government made a promise to that effect. Let me show the absurdity of the demand for a 100 per cent contribution from the dominion government. How were the old people of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia taken care of in the past? Did they starve? Were they thrown out on the dust heap? No; those provinces took care of their old people who were in need. Perhaps they did not take care of them as adequately as they can be assisted by the payment of $20 a month, but they took care of them nevertheless. And it cost them money. Did they need 100 per cent from this government to help them? They did not. They are now being offered 75 per cent by the government. Now, here is the point. Let us suppose that they do not accept it. Suppose they say they cannot afford to pay these pensions unless they get 100 per cent. Well, Mr. Speaker, in that case they will be worse off than they were before, for they will have to take care of their old people just the same, and moreover they will have to pay their share of the 75 per cent which will be paid in British Columbia and other provinces that accept the offer. On the other hand, if they decide to accept the 75 per cent and go ahead, it shows that it was not necessary to offer them more. The fact is, the government has simply made a political bargain, offering them 25 per cent too much. We are giving away the people's money to make ourselves popular with the provinces. It is so much easier, Mr. Speaker, to be generous than just. The other provinces knew that under the British North America Act they were obliged to take care of their own poor and they were glad enough to get 50 per cent. The government now say, "We are giving you

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
three million dollars more to play with", and if you lived in British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, you would know that "play" is the right word. Now that we are paying this extra money, to which the provinces are not by any process of law entitled, they ought to take care of their people between the ages of sixty-five and seventy, thus making a substantial reduction in unemployment and helping deserving old people. This extra money, spent in unemployment relief or insurance, would be better spent than handing it out to provinces who use it on the principle of- light come, light go.
To sum up again, we are only asking for justice: coal justice, grain justice, unemployment justice and, if I might put it that way, pilchard justice. What we want is plain, ordinary, common justice-not preferences or favours at the expense of anybody else. What we want is that measure of justice which from the beginning of time Providence ordained should prevail as between man and man. Man has fought and died for it ever since he was a man, and with God's help will continue to fight until he gets what he is entitled to, namely, justice.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. C. MATTHEWS (Toronto East Centre):
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not take up very much time in this house. My batting average is rather low. But I do want to say one or two things to-day with regard to some features of the budget to which reference has been made, and which possibly have not been dealt with as fully as they might have been. Before proceeding to do so, however, I think I should compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) on the splendid speech he made when delivering the budget. It was, I believe, the most comprehensive review of the affairs of Canada which I have had the pleasure of hearing or of reading. I am very doubtful whether at any time since confederation there has been brought down in this house so comprehensive a review of the affairs of the country. The budget is a different 'thing to-day from what it was years ago. Thirty years ago the presentation of the financial affairs of the country was rather a simple matter, dealing as it did with forty or fifty millions of dollars.
' Up to the beginning of the century the total revenue of Canada was, I think, always under $50,000,000-about the first of the century it crept over that figure-to-day, not only is it a complex matter in regard to finance, but the broadening interests of government and social legislation have made the budget very comprehensive. The functions of government
have increased enormously and cover a range to-day which in days gone by was not thought of. The Prime Minister has dealt with Canadian affairs in a way that has commanded the attention and met with the approval of the country. From every standpoint his speech was courageous, clear and convincing and, therefore, before proceeding further with my remarks, I would like to put myself on record as congratulating him on his excellent presentation.
The interesting thing after the budget is presented is to ascertain the course which the opposition will take, and that is particularly true this year. We have a new parliament and a new opposition; one expects the opposition to oppose because that is their function and their privilege and sometimes it is not a very difficult thing to do, but it seems to me that this year, without looking too much to an ideal, we might have had at least a suggestion of cooperation in view of the difficult times with which we are faced. I have never been able to see what was to be gained in parliament by reading for comparison different trade reports, one set dealing with depression and the other dealing with times of expansion and good business. We go pretty far in this country in the way of partisanship but there are times, and I believe this is one of them, when there might be a little cooperation for the good of the country, instead of opposition at every turn.
If any hon. member thinks that this country is suffering more than others I would advise him to go to such places as Detroit, Pittsburgh or New York, and talk with the business and professional men in those cities, talk with the bankers and with the ordinary people, find out the condition of trade and see the anxiety with which those people are looking to the future. Anyone who will do that cannot but be convinced that Canada is not in as bad a position comparatively as we are led to believe.
My own opinion is that times of expansion and depression come regardless of governments. I do not believe the fiscal policy of Canada has had much to do with the present depression, and I have never believed that. The stage was all set, it was an inevitable result following a given cause. For some years the world has been on a credit spree led by the United States. This began, as it almost always does, with very easy money conditions. Between 1921 and 1925 the United States acquired $1,500,000,000 in gold. What followed? There was an abundance of long term credit, the commercial banks discharged their indebtedness to the federal reserve sys-
The Budget-Mr. Matthews

tem and the preliminaries of expansion were clearly in evidence. There was easy credit, low rates and lack of demand for money in the domestic market in the United States. What was to be done with that extra money? With the swift enthusiasm characteristic of Americans, they went into foreign markets and began pressing loans upon foreign governments, and between 1924 and 1930, the United States loaned to foreign governments the enormous sum of $6,047,000,000. This created a credit of over six billions of dollars, which amount of spending money was placed in the hands of other nations. Naturally, much of this money was spent in the United States and it created a demand for goods such as the world had never known. The stage was all set. for the greatest boom on record. Goods manufactured and in process of manufacture were bought up and more demanded. Prosperity grew and expanded and so did the demand for credit. Industry became very prosperous and a stock market rise of long duration resulted with unprecedented profits to speculators. A very considerable percentage of the population got into the stock market and if I may be allowed to do so, I would remark that the grain market was not altogether neglected. Profits real and anticipated were used to buy more goods; thus the. stock market, the creature of prosperity, itself created more prosperity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not a written speech before me; I have notes to which I am referring; I find it very difficult to see them and perhaps that is why the hon. member thinks I am reading.
Prosperity continued to increase until the demand for credit became so great the world

over that interest rates went up and commerce and industry could not pay the rates asked for funds. The door was shut to foreign borrowing. International trade suffered to the extent of billions of dollars. Commodities declined in price. The market broke, and a depression of the first magnitude set in, which I fear is now being prolonged by influences which time does not permit me to specify.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not personally hold the view that the general situation was caused by, or very appreciably affected by, Canadian fiscal policy, although the effect of it might have been minimized if we were manufacturing our own goods, and were not the victims of dumping. But it left us in a position where business is comparatively flat, and revenues decidedly so. It is evident to everyone that more revenue must be raised to pay the expense of carrying on the government of the country. Business men know this. They expect it. There was some discussion of new taxation to take the place of the sales tax, and from hundreds of conversations I had with business men, I learned that they were all in favour of raising the sales tax-Liberals and Conservatives alike. Some have told me since the budget address that they favoured a higher sales tax than 4 per cent. They understand the tax; they wanted it; and it does not appear to me that it is a party question at all, because I am sure that if my hon. friends opposite me were in power, their first move to raise money would be to add to the sales tax-raise it as they did before.
The Prime Minister is to be congratulated on the success of the conversion loan of 14431. Asking for $250,000,000, he received $640,000,000, the strongest evidence of the faith of the Canadian people in the stability and credit of their country. Indeed, but for the desire of important holders of government bonds to keep their funds in short term liquid securities, there is no doubt that the conversion figures would have been greatly enlarged. With the knowledge of this condition, the loan can be said to have been a complete success.
The hon. the ex-Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made some comments on the conversion loan, and while he said that on the one hand there was great satisfaction in Canada that the loan had been so well received, still there was nothing extraordinary about it-it was a simple, everyday operation.

The Budget-Mr. Matthews
He also claimed that the rate of interest was not satisfactory, and pointed out that the province of Quebec a few days ago sold 7 or 8 millions of bonds on a 4.38 per cent basis; that British Columbia had made a sale on a 4.49 per cent basis; and that the state of New York tax-free serials were selling on a 3.45 per cent and 3.30 per cent basis. He did not say, however, that the Canadian tax-free bonds were selling on an equally favourable basis to those of the state of New York. In regard to his emphasis on the sale of small amounts of Canadian provincial bonds on a basis slightly more favourable than the interest on the new 4i per cent bonds, I would say that this is a matter of no significance whatever. In financial transactions one of the most important things is the magnitude. Almost any province of Canada could go into the market and dispose of a few millions on a slightly more favourable basis than that at which the dominion of Canada could expect investors to accept 600 or 700 million dollars of bonds. There is no comparison between the two cases at all, and I respectfully submit that there is no argument in the hon. gentleman's comparison in this regard.
Looking at it from a practical standpoint of marketing securities in a country with as large a territory as Canada, I am afraid the hon. gentleman is !not familiar with the difficulties to be encountered. Holders of government securities are scattered over the whole dominion, some of them in very obscure places, and the mere announcement of a conversion loan would not accomplish the desired end. I believe it was good business on the part of the government to invoke the services of the bond dealers, who would search their records for names of holders of these bonds, and get into communication with them by long distance telephone, by despatching salesmen to see them, or in other ways that would place before them the desirability of conversion. An organization was set up that was a credit to the country, and if the hon. gentleman had been sufficiently interested to ascertain the facts he would have found that the transaction was not as profitable to the sellers of the bonds as one might infer from his statements. In the first conversion loan of magnitude that the country has attempted, I think what was done was well worth the expense that attended it.
The practical effects of this conversion are very important. In the first place:
It removes from the almost immediate future the greatest financial problem that this
country has ever had before it. The clouds of financial necessity have been gathering on the horizon to the extent of more than $1,000,000,000, which required to be refunded or converted within a short time. The vast amount of government securities falling due in the early years of this decade have been referred to before in this house. As early as 1927 I drew the attention of the then Minister of Finance to the magnitude of the financing to be done. I also pointed out the disturbing influence of those clouds. Happily the Prime Minister has dissipated all fears by a most courageous and successful conversion loan, sold at par and yielding to the investor 4| per cent instead of 5 per cent and 5^ per cent, which the retiring loans bear. The removal of the greatest financial problem this country has ever faced-is one of the most encouraging steps that could be taken toward a return to better business and economic conditions.
In the second place:
The success of the conversion loan increases the nation's credit. The whole financial fabric is strengthened. The world knows that Canadians have the utmost confidence in their country and in its future, and good as the credit of Canada has been in recent years, it is even better to-day, because while other countries are having grave financial difficulties-in some cases even default has taken place, and there are suggestions of further default and repudiation filling the air-this country, through the conversion loan, has been able to take care of her own finances in a way satisfactory to her, and most creditable to her in the eyes of the world. Canada's credit has been enhanced, and the way is now open for any supplementary financing that may be necessary in connection with the retirement of the balance of the loans.
As an important Montreal paper said a few weeks ago:
If Canadians in times like these, when elsewhere there is depression and discouragement, can demonstrate their confidence in their own country's destiny by binding their fortunes to it, what is to be the effect upon Canadian credit in the eyes of the world? Can any action inspire greater confidence in Canada as a place for investment? Premier Bennett's plan is not only sound finance-it is sound psychology as well.
In the third place:
The success of this conversion lightens the public burden. Bonds that bore interest at the rate of 5 per cent and 5J per cent are being converted into securities yielding 4i per cent. I have only to give a compari-

speechtext:
I am thinking of New York.
Furthermore, the conversion raises the national revenue, because all the 4J per cent bonds are to be taxable after the date of maturity of the tax-free bonds. Perhaps this can best be illustrated by a holder wrho has, say, $10,000 of tax-free 51 per cent bonds, maturing in 1933. At the present time his income from these is $550 per annum, free of income tax. Having converted these bonds, he will have $10,000 of 4| per cent bonds, vielding annually $450. Assuming that he comes within the 25 per cent income class, his income tax on the $450 will be $112.50, which will be deducted from the $450. His net return, therefore, on the investment is $337.50, instead of $550. That is to say, the state is benefited by $100 in interest and $112.50 in income tax, or $212.50, and the investor, instead of receiving 51 per cent net, receives 3-371 per cent net on his investment, the balance going to the state.
It is axiomatic in public finance that the interests of the state surpass and transcend the interest of the investor, the holder of public securities. This results in two obligations; one on the borrower-that is, the government -and one on the investor. On the government the obligation is so to arrange maturities of funded debt that it will be in a position to take advantage of cheap time money to save interest to the state. This is accomplished by converting outstanding bonds into 
new bonds bearing a lower rate of interest. If the maturities are not so arranged, then the bonds should be made callable at prices not higher than par.
The obligation of the investor on the other hand is to recognize the right of the state to make such conversions and be prepared to accept the time loan rate on new bonds that the government might issue in exchange for the securities he holds.

The Budget-Mr. Spencer
reversed. I would like to quote a statement entitled "Impressions of U.S.A. Conditions'' by Mr. Stephen Graham, which appeared in the Manchester Guardian, and which should apply to Canada because our conditions are somewhat similar. It reads as follows:
In America, as a result of the great Wall street bubble, the rich have become much richer and the poor have become poorer, while the purchasing power of the middle class has been ruined. The abyss between the rich and the rest of the community is rapidly widening. In truth, this process was already noticeable before the slump. It is fraught with great social danger and must result in revolutionary ferment. I am not a socialist, far less a Marxian; but it is difficult to deny that capitalism as evidenced by the present _ system in America bears in itself the seeds of its own destruction.
We were informed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that some eighty-seven new factories have been established in Canada because of the policies adopted by the present government. I think it would be far better for this country if the people had a purchasing power which would enable them to buy the goods already manufactured, rather than to attempt to bring in more factories simply to create a glut of goods. As has been pointed out already, only two of these eighty-seven factories are outside the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The Minister of Trade and Commerce commented upon the wheat which had been exported by this country since this government came into power; he seemed pleased, and rather boasted of the fact that a much larger quantity had been exported this year as compared with the one previous. Does anyone in this house realize that on the exports of wheat from this country our farmers lost about 40 cents on every bushel? When that is known, I do not think it is anything to be proud of, and certainly the farmers are not shouting about it.
He made a further statement with reference to the decision of the federal government to keep used automobiles out of Canada, and mentioned that they were so numerous in the United States that they were actually being taken out in large quantities and dumped into the ocean. Now if it is the proper thing to take automobiles out and dump them into the sea, the same thing might be done with regard to manufactured goods, or food or anything else. Personally I am absolutely against such a procedure. I think that as long as there is anything that we have which the people need, whether it is food, manufactured articles or anything else, there should be some means of getting
them to the people. To-day we have poverty in the midst of plenty and such new factories as are brought into this country will only intensify the situation. I am quite sure in my own mind that the system of protection which is the policy of the government, sincere as they are, no doubt, will never be a solution for unemployment. At the same time I am frank to say that I do not think free trade is a solution, but I do think that the greater the freedom of trade that we can have, either between province and province, or internationally, the better for all concerned. Today we are in the position of having the country flooded with goods. The trouble is that we need buyers. To-day we find ourselves in the position of having, on the one hand, large quantities of goods, and, on the other hand, a lack of purchasing power, or a shortage of the medium through which to transfer one to the other. Those in control of finance appear to have no system by which sufficient money is created at any given time, to take care of the goods produced.
There are two things it seems to me to which we should devote a great deal more attention. One is the financial question, and the other the land question. I am not going to say much about the latter except that I think we shall have to take more and more of the unearned increment of land and give it to the community to whom it belongs, rather than allow it to go as at present to the speculator.
To-day we find that those who control finance are so powerful that they regulate goods to money. Rather, to my mind, the amount of goods and services in a country, that are needed by its people, should regulate the supply of the medium of exchange. Our aim should be to make it possible for the people to purchase the needed goods which can easily be produced.
Although the budget on the whole is complete in its way, more so than previous budgets, at the same time it is not as full as we should have it. For instance, I think the finance minister when he brings down his budget should give to the house a complete statement of the total annual production and the total annual consumption of goods in Canada.
Again the finance minister in his budget speech did not say anything this year about providing a solution for unemployment. Perhaps he thinks that that is not necessary, because the tariff will do it. Unfortunately as a solution I think that it will be a failure. Nor did the Minister of Finance say anything with regard to giving the people greater purchasing power, which I think is the solution
The Budget-Mr. Spencer

to a great extent. He said nothing with regard to changing the financial system, and until we do change it I do not think we have much hope of going through this crisis. He said nothing with regard to what brought on the world crisis. Although Canada is not wholly responsible for that, she has to carry her share of responsibility for any world crisis.
To-day we have what we might term an elastic yardstick with regard to money. Under the control of the present financiers there seems to be very little effort to coordinate their work, to put out sufficient of the medium of exchange at any given time.
I should like to quote two short statements in this connection, one from Lord Milner, in his book "Problems of the Hour," in which he gives one probable reason for the deflation. He says:
Just as the productive industry welcomes rising prices, the moneyed interests must always be in favour of falling prices, because they render its own wares-money-more valuable.
That is possibly one reason why we have a deflation at the present time. Again, I quote from the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna:
How car. the supply of money be increased? The amount of money in existence varies only with the action of the banks in increasing or diminishing deposits. We know how this is effected. Every bank loan creates a deposit, and every repayment of a bank loan destroys one.
Those two short statements confirm what I said, that the financiers to-day-although I think the government should have this function-largely govern the amount of money or purchasing power in. the hands of the people at any given time.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Maeleod (Mr. Coote) on the very able speech he made to this house a week ago. It contained one of the most constructive proposals we have listened to this session, and with his statements outlining it I entirely agree. I shovdd also like to bring to our support a statement by Sir Basil Blackett, a director of the Bank of England, who speaking in Ottawa some months ago and referring to the gold basis, said that there was not the slightest need for a country to hold any gold behind its currency that was used within the country, that the matter of currency and credit used by a country' as a medium of exchange should be regulated only by legislation, and that in regulating it there should be sufficient of the medium of exchange, it does not matter whether it is bank credit drawable by cheque or by currency, to enable 
the people to transfer all the goods and services needed by that nation. He said that there is a value for gold, however, in settling international balances, but even then it is looked upon as a commodity and not as coin. The Prime Minister in presenting his budget and in referring, I believe, to statements made earlier in the session by the hon. member for Maeleod, stated that we have more gold behind our currency to-day than we had a year ago, and, intimated that on that account we were so much safer. In reply to that I want to put on Hansard a brief statement from the Saturday Night of Los Angeles headed "When Gold is Unwelcome." The article is as follows:
It is estimated that the amount of gold stored in the United States is close to $4,700,000,000 and a little less than half that sum is held in France. Combined, the huge pile represents more than half the coined gold in the world. We have so much gold on hand in this country that new shipments are unwelcome, witness the arrival last week of $16,000,000 from France, much of which was derived from London and the Transvaal.
Looking to the United States we do not find conditions of enormous prosperity, in spite of their huge quantities of gold. On the other hand there is much poverty and unemployment.
Every hon. member knows that the great difficulty to-day lies in the mechanization of industry. Certainly mechanization of industry is something to be wished for; it represents a definite advance. At the same time however this same mechanization is rapidly transferring the load from the shoulders of men to machinery. The payroll of the people represents largely their purchasing power. If their work is done by machinery they are deprived of that purchasing power to buy the increased amount of goods made by machinery, and the result is an army of unemployed such as we see to-day. Unemployment coupled with money is called leisure. Unemployment without money, however, is enforced idleness and want, and there is a distinct difference. So that at each end of the scale we have unemployment. I think I am safe in saying that under our economic system all the moneys paid out to-day in the cost of production cannot possibly buy back the goods produced because, first there is inequality of income; secondly, a large amount of money is continually being put into capital investments; and thirdly, money is being reinvested in interest bearing securities. In other words our purchasing stream is being continually short circuited and the result is that there is not sufficient money to buy the goods

The Budget-Mr. Spencer
on the market. If we require money to-day we have to go to the financial houses and obtain further credits, in other words go further into debt, because when credits are advanced an equal amount of debt is created. In that connection there is one interesting point which I do not think has been sufficiently brought to the attention of the public, namely that all debts carry interest, and that interest is not payable in goods. When there is interest to pay on money, and only one place from which money can be secured when the loan or debt is to be paid, another debt has to be incurred to take care of the interest on the loan first made. So long as this situation exists we are simply multiplying debt individually, municipally, provincially and federally. A debt on a 5 per cent gilt edged security will double itself in twenty years. With reference to the position in which the farmers find themselves owing to the large interest they pay, a debt may easily double itself in fifteen years, and that is one of the reasons for the present difficulties in regard to agriculture.
Under our present system, a glut of goods is always accompanied by unemployment. As soon as a glut occurs factories shut down, and when factories are closed men are thrown out of employment. Such unemployment means lack of purchasing power, and the people who are employed have to stand the cost of those who are not employed. Purchasing power drops, prices go down and the farmer who is the least organized of all has to bear the brunt of conditions because his prices have dropped the lowest of all. Owing to the fact that my time has nearly elapsed I shall have to bring my address to a close.
I have in my hand a statement from a paper printed in England which bears the title of "Age of Plenty." This article expresses in a * few words my sentiments in regard to the financial side of the subject I have endeavoured to present to the house. I read as follows:
The amount of money in circulation to-day is not sufficient to purchase one-fifth of the goods we are able as a nation to manufacture. The present money system places industry and the people in a straitjacket, leaving no room for natural expansion. This is a condition of not being able to buy what is and could be produced in all modern countries. Hence, the struggle for foreign markets:	hence, trade
warfare, which engenders military warfare; and wars will continue as long as the present false money and economic system lasts.
Our country tries to get rid of surplus goods by methods of export. However, our country is not only a home market to ourselves but at the same time a foreign market to others.
because every country is trying to do the same thing. If, however, we have not sufficient money in the aggregate to buy the total goods made at a given time, how are we going to have money to buy imports sent to us?
Feeling as I do on this subject, Mr. Speaker, and following up the outline I have given to the house, I beg to move, seconded by Miss Macphail:
That all the words after "whereas" in the amendment be stricken out and the following substituted therefore:
This house recognizes that while certain commendable features are contained within the present budget, it is to be regretted that no provision has been made for unemployment relief, and this house further regrets the proposed decrease in the income tax as applied to the larger incomes as a retrograde step and wholly unwarranted in the present state of the national exchequer, and especially in view of the heavy additional taxation imposed upon the consumers of the country.
And whereas the general economic situation in the dominion as reflected in the financial statement contained in the present budget is extremely serious and indicates shrinking revenues consequent on business stagnation, and a tremendous decrease in commodity values accompanied by a corresponding decline in general purchasing power;
And whereas a further result of this condition is to greatly increase the burden of public and private indebtedness to a point where repayment would appear to be almost hopeless;
This house is of the opinion that the present economic conditions demand intelligent and intensive study and definite planning upon a national scale, with the view of substituting well defined cooperative principles in respect of production and distribution, together with the mobilization of our natural resources, technical equipment and financial machinery, in place of the highly competitive system under which wc are suffering at the present time.
As it is apparent that these fundamental changes cannot be put into effect in the immediate future, and that the present situation requires some prompt action.
And as the present financial situation is in many respects similar to but more serious than that which prevailed in 1914, at which time extraordinary measures were taken by the government, including the suspension of the redemption of dominion notes in gold:
This house is of the opinion that it is expedient to again suspend redemption of dominion notes in gold in order thatfa)	Commodity price levels may be raised, thus increasing the purchasing power of those engaged in agriculture, mining, forestry, fishing and other primary industries, and in this way promoting a corresponding increase in the volume of employment;
fb)	That the burden of both public and private debts and the interest thereon may be lightened:
(c)	That the amount of currency and credit available for the purposes of trade and commerce within the country, may be increased;
(d)	That through the increased volume of trade thus secured there might result larger revenues without any increase in the rate of taxation.

speechtext:
now being adopted by the administration is bound to be disastrous. What Canada needs is a moderate policy and a moderate tariff in order to bring about an exchange of goods with other nations. We must strive to bring about trade within the empire, of course, but also we must deal fairly with other countries, as we expect them to deal with us. How can we expect other countries to trade with us if we put a high tariff on all the goods they produce? That policy is bound to bring disaster.
I do not want to refer to the promises made during the last campaign; everyone is familiar with them. I do not want to refer to the promises made in my own constituency, which were perhaps even more numerous. I regret to say, however, that many of those promises have not been fulfilled. My people are still without employment; agriculture in the eastern part of Quebec has received no benefit from the budget, and there is nothing which will help our lumber industry. Last winter, in the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe, in what we call the Gaspe peninsula, there were thousands of men out of work; the shanties were all closed down, and this year all but one or two of the sawmills are closed. There is no market for the potatoes grown in the lower part of Quebec, and conditions are worse than they ever have been. I am sorry the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) and the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) are not here. The only activity in my county since the last election has been the employment of commissioners for the purpose of firing every Liberal in the county. "To the victors belong the spoils" is an old maxim; the present government have their friends, for whom they are trying to find positions, and I do not blame them. That practice has been followed by all parties. I have seen this game played from all angles; I have seen men take one stand when sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, and take a diametrically opposite stand when sitting to your left. Times change. I remember when the right hon. Prime Minister came to this house and made his debut as a promising member from western Canada, but my experience and my memory go far beyond that. I have seen a dozen governments change, and as I said before I have taken an active part in every contest since 1878. The policy has always been the same-to hold out prospects that will gather the most votes, and once you are in office try to get along as best you can.
Promises have been made which so far have not been fulfilled. There are, for example, such promises with regard to the 
railway situation. I feel it necessary to say a word in this regard because it is one of the outstanding questions at the present time. Our railways in Canada are our barometers. We have had many policies with respect to them. The government first entered upon public ownership by the construction of the Intercolonial railway. That venture was the result of confederation, and we all know how it succeeded. There was a deficit year after year and the railway had to be kept going. Then Sir John Macdonald, in his day, decided to try private ownership. He brought about the creation of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which to-day is the greatest railway company in the world. It is a world business and is an honour to Canada and to the man who brought it about. I remember, away back in 1882, listening to a speech delivered by Sir Charles Tupper in the old Queens hall in Montreal, when he came to explain the Canadian Pacific Railway contract. He could make his explanation only with the greatest difficulty, because the people were convinced, seeing that this came so soon after the Canadian Pacific scandal, that the government had sold to the Canadian Pacific Railway. In 1885 I described, for the Montreal Gazette, the first train that left Viger square station in Montreal on its way to Vancouver. Many things have happened since then. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power he had a request from western Canada to open up that country, and he was faced with a difficult railway situation. There was one line of railway and people wanted a second line. He could have done what Sir John Macdonald did: he could have incorporated a private company. But he thought he would try both private ownership and government ownership with company operation. We have not been very successful so far, but I hope that better days are coming and that many of us will remain in the land of the living to see Canada still more prosperous, because she is bound to be prosperous with all that Providence has bestowed upon her.
I uphold government ownership for the reason that there are many districts that could not be served by private railway companies. Private railways are always willing to operate in districts from which revenues are certain; they are always prepared to build railways there. But there are other districts in this country which would never pay from a railway point of view but which must have railway communication inasmuch as they contribute to the revenues of Canada. They must be served by railways. After all, the government is not a money-making concern.

The Budget-Mr. Marcil
We maintain many services that are absolutely indispensable. For example, we must keep up the postal service, we must maintain lighting services all along our coasts, we must provide life saving apparatus, and so forth. Those people who live in the remote parts of the dominion, those who are far away from the glare of the cities and who do not enjoy the luxuries which are available to the people of central Canada, must have means of communication with the rest of the country. Take for example, Mr. Speaker, the people who live in the far west in the constituency you represent, or those who live in the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this house. These people must be given their fair share of the good things that are available, and to this end railway communication is necessary in parts of Canada that would not be served by private enterprise. The Gaspe peninsula, for example, is the oldest part of Canada. There in 1534, four hundred years ago, Jacques Cartier, the discoverer of this country, planted the Cross of Christ in the old town of Gaspe and opened up this land of Canada which has since become one of the greatest countries in the world. Without government ownership of railways such parts of the country would never be served.
Now that we are having a hard time with our railways there is a question of merging the two. I should be opposed to that from early morning until late at night. Monopolies are to be feared in this country; they are to be feared in railways as in trade. Imagine a government in office with a single railway system dominating the whole country: what a monopoly, wffiat a merger that would be. We would not stand for it; the country would not stand for it.
There was some question, when the Liberal party came into office in 1901, as to the stand it would take with respect to government ownership. The Canadian National Railways, as we know the system, is the creation of the Conservative party, and I must give credit to the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen for the splendid work he did in that connection. He certainly rendered valuable services to the country, because on the downfall of the Mackenzie-Mann regime, we found ourselves in a difficult position. On coming into office in 1921 we found a deficit of $60,000,000 a year, and it certainly needed some courage to bring about public ownership. However, that gentleman did the best he could, and government ownership is still on trial. Government ownership will be successful when things improve. When the country is prosperous the Canadian National Railways will feel the effects just as will the Canadian Pacific. If the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway can afford to lose a portion of their dividends in the hard times through which we are now passing, the Canadian people, as shareholders in the national system, can at least face the situation in the same spirit.
There are other things I should like to have touched upon but time will not permit. I am sorry the government has taken the retrograde step it has in regard to the penny postage. Penny postage was the work of Sir William Mulock, now the leading citizen of Ontario, in the highest court of which province he has the honour of presiding. He was immensely proud, and he had reason to be, of the fact that he was the father of penny postage, which advertised Canada throughout the world. We sent letters throughout the empire and the system which he established has been of very considerable advantage to the country at large. WThen he took over the department with three cent postage there was a huge deficit, and in the course of a few years there was a large surplus. He extended the postal service, opening thousands of offices. When I was first elected there were post offices in Canada, the postmasters being paid $10 a year. This was increased to S25, then $35, and later on to ?60; and finally, under the late administration, the rate was increased to $100.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the facilities afforded by the postal service for communication with the outside world are the only means which very many people have of getting in touch with what is going on in other parts of the country. There are people who live far from railways and they' must therefore depend upon correspondence. And the low rate of postage encourages correspondence. One cent additional on a letter does not seem much, but for poor people who have many letters to write it is a considerable item; they will think twice before writing. I regret this retrograde step on the part of the government; penny postage should have been allowed to stand. Canada has set an example to the rest of the world in many things, and this is one institution to which we should have adhered.
Shall I mention old age pensions and unemployment? The house is familiar with these topics; I will not take up time discussing them. Nor will I discuss butter. Why are there so many members opposite representing the province of Quebec to-day? Quebec is a dairy province and in my own constituency there is a butter factory in every
The Budget-Mr. Marcil

parish. In the last election the promise was made openly-not by the leader of the Conservative party, because he would not make such a promise, but by members of the party -that if hon. gentlemen opposite were returned to power butter would sell at 40 and 50 cents per pound as soon as the New Zealand treaty was done away with. Well, in Bonaventure to-day the farmers are receiving 15 cents per pound while eggs are being sold at 10 cents a dozen. Pulpwood is not selling at all. And as regards fish, the people are drying their fish or salting it, waiting for better prices later on.
Another promise made was in connection with the old age pensions. This promise was broadcast in the province of Quebec, and in my own constituency canvassers went from house to house making the formal promise on behalf of the incoming administration that there would be an old age pension paid of which the federal government would pay one hundred per cent. The province of Quebec is one of the oldest provinces in the dominion. The position there is somewhat different from that pertaining in the other provinces. We have many religious institutions for the purpose of looking after the lame, the infirm, the blind, the orphan and the old man and woman; we are equipped already with institutions to look after all classes of unfortunates, and to knock down and destroy this system overnight is an act which should receive serious consideration. The provincial government has appointed a royal commission to make a report on these institutions, but in the meantime Quebec will have to pay 75 per cent of the cost of these pensions, whereas the other provinces have to pay only 50 per cent.
I thank the house for the patient attention it has given to my remarks. The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has been working night and day, and in my opinion there has never been a public man who has applied himself so devotedly to the public interest as has the right hon. gentleman. I hope he is equal to the task, and I trust he will live long enough to admit the great mistake which he has made. I hope that many of these resolutions which bear so heavily upon the poorer classes will be modified before they are presented to the house.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
