speechtext:
May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to extend to the hon member for Bona venture (Mr. Marcil), who has just taken his seat, a very sincere tribute to one who by the fairness and courtesy with which he always addresses the house sets an example which we young and newer members might well follow. The hon. member is, I believe, with the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), one of the oldest members of this house, and one can see from the very able manner with which at this time, after thirty years of public life, he has addressed the house, why he has continued to represent the one constituency continuously for thirty years. I trust that he may continue for the rest of his life, if he so desires, to represent that constitnency, even though it be on the opposite side of the house. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might also be allowed to pay a tribute to the Minister of Justice, who has sat in this house for thirty years and has devoted the best years of his life to the public service of this country.
It is with considerable diffidence that as a new member I rise to speak in a budget debate. First let me join with the other members of the house in extending to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) my most sincere congratulations upon the very comprehensive financial statement which accompanied his address. It is something which the new members of the house appreciate very much as it affords a basis upon which calculations may be made when future budgets are brought down. The Prime Minister's budget speech sets forth in one concentrated statement a true picture of the financial position of the country.
The first thing which strikes one with respect to a budget is whether there is a deficit or a surplus. This budget shows a deficit of some 884,000,000. It is rather interesting to note that when the previous administration came into power in 1921 they were faced with almost the same deficit, amounting as it did to some $S1,000,000. It does seem to me, and I think I am fair in saying this, that the deficit with which the present administration is faced is not attributable to the government now in power. I think that is clear. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) frankly admitted this afternoon that this government could not be held responsible for that deficit.

The Budget

Mr. Bowman
A glance at an item or two will clearly show how the deficit did arise. First of all there was a reduction in the receipts of customs revenue of $48,000,000, which was evenly distributed over the first six months and the latter months of the year, the details of which are given in the budget speech. There was a drop of $7,000,000 in excise duties on alcoholic beverages. I think perhaps the King administration should be given some credit for that, rather than be charged with a portion of the deficit there. There was some $24,000,000 less in sales tax, and $3,000,000 less in post office revenue. These items total $82,000,000. There was increased expenditure on account of old age pensions amounting to $4,000,000, $5,000,000 for subsidies to Manitoba, $7,000,000 for war pensions and after care, and $4,000,000 for unemployed relief. These reductions in receipts and increases in expenditure total $102,000,000. I am not attempting to show the exact debits and credits. I am showing in a very simple manner the financial situation with which this government has been faced.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) stated that there was something which this budget did not contain, namely, a surplus. Quite true, but there were budgets of the former administration which did not contain a surplus, If we go back to the year 1922, we find the following-I quote from the public accounts of last year:

That table shows a total increase of debt during those years of $112,897,885.05 and a total decrease of debt of $276,012,910.03 making a total net decrease of debt during that period of nine years of $163,115,024.98. It might be noted that the increase of debt for 1931, without taking into consideration the write-off which was allowed for in the matter of soldiers' loans and so forth, was $83,844,358.
So this government to-day stands very much iD the same position in which the former administration stood when it came into office. There had been a period of deflation following the war, and our citizens from one end of the country to the other were facing hardships. Times were difficult. In the west the farmers were burdened with debt, having purchased land at high prices. Conditions were almost the same as those with which the country is faced to-day, and it is rather a remarkable coincidence that when the King administration took office in 1921 they were faced with a deficit which was almost the same as that with which this government is faced.
Being faced with this deficit, the government of the day had to do one of two things. The deficit was there, and the government either had to capitalize that indebtedness and go on collecting the same taxes they had in the past, or levy increased taxation if they were to make the budget balance. There is a very notable silence on the other side of the house in that regard. Nobody on the other side has suggested that that deficit be capitalized; not at all. That was done in the United States, but we in Canada have apparently made up our minds that we are going to pay our way as long as we can, and in arriving at that decision I think the government adopted the proper course.
There is another similarity between what happened when the King administration came into power and the conditions prevailing when the present government took office. I refer to the manner in which a deficit was guarded against in the following year. We find that the King administration levied very much the same additional taxes that this government is levying to-day, yet we hear objections from hon. members on the other side of the house. Mind you, we hear objections, but not one constructive suggestion of any kind looking to the substitution of fairer or more equitable taxes.
As might have been expected, this of course was termed the rich man's budget. No hon. member on this side of the house expected to hear anything else. That has been the cry from time immemorial. In 1925 the cry was, "If you put the Conservative party in power you are placing St. James street in power." To-day we are faced with the criticism that the budget now under consideration is a rich man's budget. I say no government in Canada to-day would dare to bring in a budget favouring the rich man, and I say further that this government has not done so. During the short session last fall the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that the legislation then enacted favoured special interests and capitalists. Turning to page 419 of Hansard of the special session I find Mr. King stated that the tariff legislation favoured special interests. He said, "It
The Budget-Mr. Bowman

is apparent that the capitalist, the man who had his capital invested, has benefited." Unfortunately. however, the right hon. leader of the opposition went too far and in an attempt to prove his argument, placed figures on Hansard. He asked hon. members to look at the stock market and to consider Dominion Textile, Coekshutt Plough and Steel of Canada He said that the low figure for the year of the Dominion Textile stock had been $61, that when the Conservative government assumed power it. had gone up to $70, and on September 16, two days before the time the right hon. leader of the opposition spoke, it had gone up to $84.50. He attempted to show how special interests and capitalists had been favoured. May I ask the right hon. leader of the opposition what he says to-day when the stock has gone down to $66.25? He went on to state at that time that the low figure in 1930 for Coekshutt Plough had been 14 J. On July 28, the day of the elections the stock stood at 16L and on the 16th of September when the tariff resolutions were introduced it stood at 20J. I wonder what the right hon. gentleman has to say now that that stock is quoted at only 51? Giving the figures for Steel of Canada he said that the low figure for 1930 had been 39J, that on July 28 last year, it had stood at 45 and on September 16 had risen to 47; to-day this stock is down to 26J. Is that the way the special interests and capitalists have been favoured by this government?

It is the ordinary, everyday consumers, the men and women who are hard put to make ends meet, men who are out of work, who are now called upon to pay the extra amount in connection with the sales tax. Out of $78,000,000 in additional taxation the sum of $52,000,000 will be raised by the sales tax alone.

Taking out the first 'and last year we have a total collected (during the nine years of the King administration of $657,414,832. I wonder how the King administration would have obtained their net surplus of $163,000,000 if they had not levied the sales tax which they are now condemning? If we take the total figure levied for the nine year period just mentioned and divide it by nine, we find that over that period there was an average sales tax collected from the people of Canada of about $73,000,000 per year, or at least a million dollars every year they were, in power more than this government proposes to collect in the coming fiscal year. To divide the total figure by eleven to cover the total number of years I have mentioned, we get the figure of about $65,000,000 which has been collected yearly since the first year the sales tax was imposed. So that after all we are not dealing with a new form of taxation. It is not an unfair tax, if we are to judge fairness by what has taken place under other administrations. At this point it may be noted that in May, 1930, when the late administration was preparing for the election, about $24,000,000 was lopped off this tax. I presume that if the sales tax was fair under the. former administration it is equally fair under the present one.
For a moment let us consider the income tax. Again we are told the budget we are now considering is a rich man's budget because it favours the. very, very rich. I do not 'believe that is a fact and I have made rather a close examination of the provisions contained in the budget. This afternoon a very able address was delivered by the hon. member for Toronto East Centre (Mr. Matthews). I regret I was not in the house during the first part of his speech, and if I duplicate what he has said I hope hon. members will excuse me. In connection with the sales tax we have what appears to be an attempt by hon. members opposite to show that we are dealing with a rich man's budget. I am rather

The Budget-Mr. Bowman
surprised that a man like the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth should have made the following statement, which is contained at page 2302 of Hansard:
The next point is the elimination of the forty-nine per cent maximum. Formerly large incomes were taxed to a maximum of forty-nine per cent.
Note the repetition.
Under the new Income Tax Act, for some reason which has not been explained as yet, the maximum to which an income can be taxed is twenty-five per cent.
The implication clearly being that under the old act there is a tax of approximately fifty per cent, but that under the new act you have a tax of only twenty-five per cent. I do not accuse the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth of deliberately making an incorrect statement, but undoubtedly he has done so. There was the ten per cent reduction in income tax in 1927, and a similar reduction in 1928. So the maximum tax was not forty-nine per cent as stated by the hon. member, but forty per cent.
Personally I have no hesitation in saying that I am against favouring any multi-millionaire. But as I read the numerous changes in the Income Tax Act I fail to see wherein they favour the rich man, and I will explain why. First of all, let me deal briefly with the exemptions on the lower incomes. The exemption in the case of a married man is increased by $500, so that a married man with a family of three children now enjoys an exemption of $5,000-and every married man should have at least three children.

The exemption in favour of a single man is increased by $250, giving him a total exemption of $1,750. And there is this significant fact, that by those changes 25,000 out of approximately the 135,000 people estimated to be subject to income tax are now entirely exempt from this tax. Those changes in the Income Tax Act at least do not favour the rich. Another 75,000 with incomes between $5,000 and $10,000 have their income tax reduced. Roughly speaking, the income tax is increased on incomes starting at $10,000 and going up to $130,000. I do not know how it is in other ridings, but in my district a man who has an income of $10,000 is considered to be pretty well off, and when he gets up to $25,000 or $50,000 we look upon him as a wealthy man, but when he enjoys an income of $75,000 to $100,000 we consider him to be a very wealthy man indeed. Well, the income tax on all incomes from $10,000 to $130,000 has 22110-162
been increased, which is as it should be. So there is no favouritism to the rich man there. With respect to incomes over $140,000 there is a decrease-I have not figured out exactly what it amounts to-but there is something which offsets that decrease. Some peculiar statements have been made in this house during the course of this debate regarding income tax. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) speaking on June 4, is reported at page 2321 of Hansard as saying that:
There is also a group of about twenty-five citizens who are taxed on a revenue of $1,000,000 or more yearly.
May I say to the hon. member that for the last ten years not a single person in Canada has been paying income tax on $1,000,000 yearly-not one; and last year not a single taxpayer paid the tax on an income of over $500,000. I do not think hon. members should make such statements without being mighty sure that they are right. Of course they may be made with the idea of showing that this is in reality a rich man's budget. The hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) is reported at page 2502 of Hansard in these words:
But what happens to a man with an income of $50,000 per year? Under the old income tax he had to pay $10,530 more.
I do not know where the hon. member got those figures, but as a matter oif fact under the old act that man paid $6,704 while under the new act, instead of a decrease as stated by the hon. gentleman there is an increase of about $1,900, and on that income the correct tax actually is $8,615. But the hon. member goes further and says:
According to the 1929 return there were 523 in this country who were in receipt of an income this large or larger. If these men were taxed as they were taxed previously-
According to his figures.
-it wrould increase the revenue of the public treasury by over $5,500,000.

If he has sense, yes. If a lot of us had our money in the conversion loan we would be better off. I say that a tax on people rvho put their money into corporations is a tax against the rich man. Then the family corporation is now wiped out altogether. All you had to do formerly was to incorporate yourself, your wife, son, daughter, cousins or other relations and you escaped the eight per cent corporation tax. That has 'been wiped out. Is that in favour of the poor man or of the rich man?
Personal corporations came in Canada a few years ago from the old country I believe.
I admit that the evasion of income tax as permitted by these corporations was largely done away with by the 1026 amendments to the Income Tax Act, but those personal corporations are now w'holly abolished so far as income tax payments are concerned. Then in addition to all these charges the rich man has to pay, when a company is wound up or a merger goes into effect, a direct charge of. four per cent on as much of the sale price as can be classified as income, and that must be taken out before the transfer is legally complete. It is extremely difficult for one to foretell what will be collected under an income tax act, but I think we will all agree that while 'there may be the provisions to which I have referred which will assist the immensely rich man, there are others which more than compensate for that.
In concluding my argument with respect to the income tax, may I point out that the old act has been abolished. A new act is being put into effect, giving power to the excise officers to go into every detail of the finances of the individual or corporation in order to see that everything is paid that should be paid. Personally I have no hesitation, therefore, in supporting this administration with respect to its income tax proposals.
Then there is the question of the tax on cheques under S10. One would imagine it was something new. It must be borne in mind that for five and a half of the nine years of the previous administration we had to put stamps on cheques under $10. Surely we can get along with it a little longer. Who really pays that tax? I will admit that the tax should be wiped out with regard to cream cheques. But who really does pay it? Is it not largely paid by the business and professional man? It is not paid by the poor man. Most of us are glad these days to have a cheque to stamp.
There is also the increased postage. Why should there not be an increase in the postal

rate from two to three cents? The Post Office Department is faced with a deficit of $6,100,000, so why should it not try to make up that deficit? I think it is being done in the proper way. In the statement made by the Prime Minister in this house he said that the rates on newspapers and magazines were to be increased, that the treasury of this country had lost millions of dollars in handling newspapers and magazines below cost. Why should not the newspaper concerns of this country pay at least the actual cost of transportation? With regard to the duty on magazines, I think that this is a mighty fine thing. This country will be a whole lot better off without many of the trashy magazines which come in from the United States; they should be barred from this country forever.
Just for a moment I should like to deal with unemployment. No one in this house can speak too strongly with respect to conditions of employment as they exist in Canada to-day, but I believe things are at their worst. We may have a bad winter ahead of us; I am quite frank in saying that I believe we will, and I think this government should marshal its resources in order to relieve the poor and needy of Canada. I do not think any man will begrudge extra taxes in order to relieve the poor or starving people, particularly at a time when our granaries are filled with wheat and other grains. However, I think there is some hope. These periods of depression come in cycles. The Prime Minister pointed out in his speech that a great number of business concerns had located in this country since last August. If conditions in Ontario and Quebec improve, that will help the west; perhaps we might envy you a little, but nothing more. We hope old Ontario and Quebec will'come back with a bang. Give the west decent prices for her wheat and you will see how quickly we can come back.
There is one thing for which I think this government should be given credit. Within seven days after they took office they passed an order in council restricting immigration. Allow me to give the figures in that respect. Beginning with September of 1929-30 and 1930-31, the immigration figures are as follows:

My time is about up, and I hasten to deal briefly with one or two other matters. Mention was made by the Prime Minister of the sum of $1,225,000 being expended in connection with air mail service. Let me say emphatically that at a time like this, when every letter sent by air mail costs $30 it is time we cut out the air mail service. The Prime Minister has indicated that notices of cancellation of the contracts have been sent out, and I trust that they will not be renewed, or that if renewed will be on a more equitable basis.
There is the question of old age pensions, in connection with which the federal contribution has been increased from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. Last year the province of Manitoba paid $670,275 in old age pensions, and this increased contribution by the federal treasury will mean a direct saving to Manitoba of some $335,000. That will be a saving to every farmer and every taxpayer which will be much appreciated. I trust that by the time another session is called we will get the other 25 per cent promised by the Prime Minister.
I have not time to deal with the tariff changes, except to say that speaking for my own province, and I think also for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the increase in the tariff on corn is welcome. I trust that the people in the east and in British Columbia will make a real test of feeding barley and observe carefully the results. I will say this for the people of the west: If barley does not prove a satisfactory feed for the poultry of British Columbia and the hogs of Ontario and Quebec, then the people of the west will say, take off the tariff and import corn. That is as fair a proposition as I can make. Let me remind hon. gentlemen from British Columbia that the people on the prairies purchase coal and fruit from that province.

speechtext:
One of the
unfortunate effects of the forty minute rule is that it precludes a member from following the one who has immediately preceded him: that is, if he is to give the speech he has himself prepared. I shall not at the moment say anything in regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman), although a little later on I do expect to refer to one matter he dealt with.
It would seem to be the custom to extend congratulations, and I should like to congratulate both the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). Both of these hon. gentlemen dealt with the economic conditions of the country in a very comprehensive way: that at least is one quality they had in common. But here the similarity ends. The Prime Minister naturally ascribed to his predecessors all the evils of the present time and took credit to himself for any bright spots that might exist; and naturally, also, he emphasized his own policies as the ones that were likely to bring prosperity to the people of Canada. Naturally the hon. member for Shelbtirne-Yarmouth dissented from those views; in large measure he ascribed the present conditions to the policies of the government now in office and contended that if that government were to continue pursuing those policies it would mean disaster. As between the two, I have no hesitation in saying that I heartily agree with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth.
In another respect we might congratulate the Minister of Finance. The budget is not as bad as it might have been. We had been given reason to believe that the whole scale of customs items would be raised all along the line. That has not been done and I wonder what the reason is. The reason may be found, perhaps, in the physical inability of the Minister of Finance to accomplish that work, and the fact, perhaps, that he is somewhat hesitant about making a change the effects of which he cannot foresee-such a change, for instance, as that in respect to the glass duty of unholy memory with which the hon. member for West Hamilton was so closely associated. The reason the budget is not as bad as it might have been may be
2548
The Budget-Mr. Brown

however, that possibly the shadow of a doubt crept into the mind of the Minister of Finance as to the effect of that cure-all which he has presented to the people, that panacea that is to remedy all the ills of the body politic. If such be the case, I am sure it will be very welcome to us on this side to learn that there was that shadow of a doubt as to the efficacy of the right hon. gentleman's policy. We should certainly be very much pleased to discover that in his mind and in the minds of his followers there was such a doubt.
Something else upon which I would congratulate the Minister of Finance is that he has evidently come to a recognition of the fact that the volume of revenue does not necessarily depend upon the rate of taxation, or at least that the rate of taxation is not the only factor in determining the volume of revenue. We have listened for the past four or five years to speeches from hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were on this side of the house, denouncing the government of the day for the large volume of revenue. Again and again they complained of the vast sums taken out of the pockets of the people through taxation. That was the complaint they were making. Now they are faced with a deficit, the complaint is that the former government reduced taxation. Turning to the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) I find that he pointed to the fact that, faced with a deficit, the Hon. Mr. Dunning had in the last parliament reduced taxation. I believe the minister used the expression that Mr. Dunning had interfered with a number of sources of taxation. That has been emphasized a number of times in the course of this debate. The hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Baker) referred to the same fact and claimed that instead of reducing the sales tax by 1 per cent last year the government of that day should have increased it. It is rather amusing to us on this side of the house now to hear new members -the old ones would scarcely dare to do it- declaiming against the reduction of the sales tax last year, when we remember the attitude of those on the opposite side of the house during a number of years: they contended that the sales tax should be completely wiped out. It is a wonderful illustration of the way circumstances alter cases.
As I have said, the Minister of Finance has evidently learned, speaking generally, that all he is able to do is to fix the rates of taxation, for the volume of taxation will be determined by the amount of business that is done when those different rates are in effect. The right hon. gentleman contended-and hon. members
[M Brown. 1
opposite supported him in the contention- that the government of the day was responsible for the volume of revenue that accrued from the imposition of particular rates of taxation. At page 2168 of Hansard, now he says:
On the basis of existing taxation rates, the anticipated revenues in the present fiscal year will be $325,120,000.
And on page 2169, he says:
On the basis of the present volume of business, it is estimated that these additional taxes will yield $94,000,000 in a twelve months period.
It is worth something if hon. gentlemen opposite have learned that maximum rates do not necessarily produce the maximum amount of business, and certainly not the maximum amount of revenue. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking on the income tax, said, as reported at page 2312:
My second point is this: that a sound tax must result in revenue to the country; otherwise, it is not desirable.
I think it would be well for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to carry that argument into other fields of taxation and to remember that a tax is not sound unless it produces revenue. If hon. gentlemen opposite would apply that principle when dealing with tariff matters, they would perhaps realize that high rates of tariff taxation do not necessarily increase the amount of revenue. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that revenue is the last thing in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Last September we had a short session and went into committee of ways and means. According to my understanding of committee of ways and means, parliament is supposed to consider means of raising revenue to carry on the government of the country. And yet during the session of last fall no one gave the slightest thought to the effect upon the revenues of the country of the tariffs which they were imposing. I think the same principle is very largely true of the present tariffs.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) took occasion to taunt those who sit on this side of the house with the fact that they never would say at just what point they wanted the tariff fixed. I think we might very well retort that hon. members on his side of the house have never stated at what point they want the tariff fixed or how much consideration they will give to the questions of revenue and protection. The maximum amount of tariff will not produce the maximum amount of revenue.

The Budget-Mr. Brown
For a few moments I would like to deal with the income tax. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce sought to justify the exemptions on dividends up to a certain amount on the ground that this tax is being paid by wealthy men. He urged that wealthy men put their money into these corporations, and that the tax on the corporation also was a tax on the wealthy man. We distinguish between the wealthy man as an individual and the wealthy man as a member of a corporation. This country is not composed of corporations, it is composed of individual men and women. I do not intend to speak against the tax on corporations or contend that the government is wrong in imposing it, other than to point out that this corporation tax is a tax on the doing of business and in a great many instances it is counted simply as overhead and is passed along to the consumer either for the services or the products furnished by the corporation. That may not be true in every case, but it certainly is true in a large number. I believe that the individual citizens of this country should bear their share of taxation and they ought to bear it in proportion to their ability to pay. Much has been said about this being a Christian country; many hon. members opposite have stated that we should not deal with Russia because it is not a Christian country. While I have not urged my views very strongly in the past, I do remember 'the statement:
. . . .unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
I think that rule could be applied in connection with the income tax. If ability has been given to a man to accumulate great wealth, that should be considered as one of the talents given to him to be employed for the general good.
I would refer the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) to the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. While defending the changes in the income tax the minister admitted that it was relieving the wealthy man. He said that that had been done because heavy taxation was driving capital out of the country. The hon. member for Dauphin and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce should get together and try to reconcile their views upon that point.
I am not at all impressed by what has been said with reference to double taxation. As I have said, corporations are one thing and individual taxpayers are another. The fact that a person with an income of $10,000 from dividends is granted exemption does not appeal to me at all. Much has been said in the past about the hypothetical widow who might
have a few thousand dollars left to her by her husband and who would be unjustly taxed by having to pay on those dividends. I am not very much concerned about a hypothetical widow who has an income of $10,000, but I am concerned about the widows out on the prairies. Some of the constituents of the hon. member for Dauphin have no hope of ever having an income of $10,000 per year; they are forced to count every cent and see that it is used to the very best advantage. I have very little sympathy with the objections made to double taxation.
I listened with some interest to the remarks of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with the conversion loan. We are all glad that that loan was a success, but after all it was a comparatively simple piece of financing. It was a large transaction it is true, but it was very simple in its essential elements. It was recognized that some provision would have to be made in regard to the debt of this country-Mr. Dunning mentioned it last year during the course of his budget speech when he said that special attention would have to be given by the government to the obligations which were maturing. The very period of depression through which we are passing made the financing of this loan an easier matter. Why? The people had no place else to put their money. An article which appeared in the Atlantic Monthly states that time money is bringing only two per cent, and call money only li per cent. It is not hard to understand why men should be quite willing to exchange bonds bearing 5i per cent interest for those bearing 41 per cent interest. We are glad it turned out in the way it did, but, as I have said, it was a comparatively simple transaction and the circumstances of the day lent themselves to it in a special measure.
During the course of his remarks the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth Mr. Ralston) stated in connection with the automobile industry that the public got the benefit of the application of the tariff of 1926 and that the automobile industry was not hurt. The hon. member for East Essex (Mr. Morand) undertook to combat that statement, and I would refer to the argument which he advanced on that occasion. Every car that was manufactured in Canada gave $456 worth of work to some Canadian workman.
I suppose that statement meets with the approval of hon. members opposite. It proves, however, what I have already said, that in the minds of my hon. friends opposite revenue is the last consideration. If an importation of 44,053 in 1929 was too great an import, how many should have come in? Do hon. members wish to shut out entirely our imports of automobiles?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says,
"surely." Well then, from where will we get our revenue? My hon. friend says, "Shut out entirely the importation of automobiles." All right, but whence shall we derive the revenue? If we are to shut out entirely the importation of automobiles why bother about juggling the rate of discount or fixing value for duty purposes? Now let us be honest about the matter and say we will not import any automobiles, that we will place an embargo on them. If hon. gentlemen opposite take the position that the importation of automobiles should be stopped, let them take that position. If on the other hand an importation of 44,000 in one year is too many, let them say how many should come in.
I cannot allow the occasion to pass without saying a word or two concerning the proposal to pay 5 cents a bushel on export wheat. Frankly, it is a kind of legislation that I do not like, but under the circumstances I do not think it is any more than is coming to the farmers of the northwest. The grain growers more than anybody else have suffered from the great depression that has overtaken the country. I do not know how the government is going to apply this freight rate adjustment to wheat destined for export and not to wheat used for home consumption. I am afraid that it is a problem that they will have difficulty in solving. Indeed, the only way in which that benefit can be assured to the farmer is to pay a bounty on all wheat, whether for export or for home consumption. I believe that is the only way by which you

The Budget-Mr. Picket
can foe certain that the money will go to the farmer and that no other person will benefit. In regard to the duty on corn, I assert the position that I have assented so often in this house: I do not believe that ultimately the farmer can benefit by the application of the principle of protection, and he is foolish when he falls for it.
Now, if there is one thing more foolish than another on the part of this government it is their dumping legislation. Perhaps one of the funniest things that has happened is the order in council changing the tariff item from "potatoes" to "radishes." I think the Prime Minister has but little sense of humour. Hon. members will recall the puzzle sometimes seen in the newspapers, known as letter golf, in which by making a change letter by letter you eventually form a new word. The Prime Minister has gone one better; he managed to change potatoes to radishes at one move. This agility of his reminds me of another story. Two Swedes had agreed to go aboard a boat at a certain time. Ole got aboard. Yonnie came running down the hill just as the boat was pulling away from the wharf. Ole shouted to him, "Yonnie, yump, yump. You can make it in two yumps." If the Prime Minister could show as much agility in athletics as he does in changing tariffs he would have made it in one "yump."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until the .first of this month it had never been my good fortune to listen to a budget speech in this house, but I had read many of them. To my mind the budget brought down by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is the best resume of the financial condition and structure of this country that I have ever read. It goes into the whole subject in detail, shows us our indebtedness, our income and our expenditure, and makes provision for increased revenue.
Before proceeding further I should like to make one or two corrections of statements by the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). Some time ago in a speech delivered in this house he referred to what I said about the increased number of factories in my riding. I did not intend to convey the idea that all those factories were built as a result of the tariff policy of this government. I simply stated that some of them had closed down and that after the special session last September they had begun to function again. I made no reference whatever to the Vilas Company at Cowansville, I merely referred to the largest sign manufacturing company in Canada which doubled their capacity and the number of their employees after the September session.
I congratulate the members who have already taken part in this debate for the high order of their speeches, but I am afraid I will not be able to maintain the standard they have set. Particularly do I desire to mention the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and the hon. member for Bona venture (Mr. Marcil) for the moderation of their criticism. In addition to the moderation of his speech I think the hon. member for Bonaventure gave the house a very fine historic review covering the last thirty years.
If, as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth stated, those on his side of the house are sincere in their convictions, I want to assure him that we on this side are just as sincere, and all we ask is that we be allowed to give our policies a thorough trial. From our point of view this country has suffered for many years from lack of the policies that we advocate. Never since 1878 until last September have we had a man at the helm of affairs who had the stamina and the backbone to carry out his convictions.
As the hon. member for Bonaventure stated, in 1878 things were pretty flat in Canada. I can remember that cheese was selling at 5 and 6 cents a pound and butter at 10 and 12 cents a pound, and the outlook indeed was blue. The commercial treaty of 1866 had been abrogated by the United States, and their action put us in the hole. In 1878 the national policy was enunciated, and Sir John A. Macdonald stated that it would bring about the development of industries in this country. And it did; factories were erected and we began to manufacture. At that time the agricultural community objected to protection, and for years afterwards there was a large class in this country who did oppose the national policy. For that reason I suppose the tariff was never increased as it should have been.; rather there was a tendency on the part of Liberal governments to reduce the tariff a trifle. But at the present time there is no doubt the farming community are perfectly in accord with the tariff policy of this government. They have seen the need of protection, and they feel that great good may come to this country out of the evil done to our dairy industry by the Australian tariff treaty. Up to that time our farmers did not think they required protection. But they did. From 1900 to 1914 tons of American butter and American pork were dumped into this country, carload after carload, and the farmers did not for a moment think of protection. These products should have been protected, in which event the income of the agricultural com-
The Budget-Mr. Picket

munity would have been materially increased. After experiencing hard times since 1925, the date of the Australian trade treaty, the farmer is a thorough convert to protection. He knows he requires it in his business. From a country exporting 27,000,000 pounds of butter we became, in five or six years, a country importing about 50,000,000 pounds, or almost one-third the amount of butter manufactured in this country.
Much has been said about the old cow- and I am sorry the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) is not here. Much has been said about butter, and on this side of the house we admit that Australian and New Zealand butter was the lubricant which slipped the Liberal party out of power. We admit also that if we do not do something for the farmer that same lubricant will be used to slip us out. For once the farmers of this country were united; they spoke as one man. They asked for protection; they require it; they demand it, and they must have it. We must keep for the Canadian agriculturist the Canadian butter market, and also the egg market, the cheese market and the meat market. Notwithstanding the fact that we have lost our bacon market in England, to which we shipped formerly one hundred million pounds; notwithstanding the fact that we brought in $30,000,000 worth of meat and meat products from the United States, the bureau of statistics tries to tell us that we have a great many more hogs, that we produce more eggs and more bacon, but that we are consuming our own products. I do not know how they arrive at that conclusion; I should like to know how they take the census of these commodities. I know in my section of the country, and all through the eastern townships, we have only 25 per cent of the hog population we had seven or eight years ago, and this is so all through the province of Quebec. I will grant that probably there are more in the west; probably the hog population in that part of the country has increased, but on the whole we have lost markets for meat and meat products, butter, eggs and cheese. New Zealand has ousted us from those markets.
As far as the tariff is concerned, I should like to quote just a few figures with regard to imports. Of iron and steel, and iron and steel products, we imported over $350,000,000 worth; of agricultural implements, more than $35,000,000; of agricultural products, over $72,000,000, and of textiles over $137,000,000. In this country we are quite capable of producing three-quarters of these commodities and thereby giving employment to many

thousands of workmen. If we had adopted a sane policy of protection in this country there is no reason why to-day we should be helping the unemployed.
Hon. members opposite have laid great stress on the fact that for the past five or six years we have had great prosperity. What are the facts? Let us look at the amount of money spent in connection with immigration. In round figures the expenditure by years was;

What was the result? During that same period we lost over 1,200,000 people. During that great period of prosperity we spent over $26,000,000 on immigration and lost 1,200,000 people, who went from Canada to the United States to seek an opportunity to make a living, which was denied them here. These are the facts. It seems to me that during that period of great prosperity we should have been giving employment to those people here, and should have been making conditions in this country more livable so that people would come here without being bought. That should be the immigration policy; we should make our country livable so that people will want to come here without being paid.
The tariff policy, to my mind, should encourage competition, but not, as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) stated, external competition; it should protect our home industries in such a way as to encourage competition at home. That is the kind of competition we want, competition among our own manufacturers which will keep down prices. The west complains a great deal about the cost of manufactured goods, but I should like to tell hon. members from the west that they are going through the same experience endured by the western part of the United States in the seventies and eighties. It will not be long, as the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Stanley) said yesterday, before manufacturers will be located in the west, and the farmers will be able to buy a mowing machine, a plough or a harvester just as cheaply as these articles can be bought in the east. That is what we want; we should like to decentralize our manufacturers and spread them over the country where they will do the greatest amount of good.

The Budget-Mr. Gershaui
Last year, the year ended March 31, 1930, we sent nearly $900,000,000 into the United States. Mr. Speaker, there is one great consolation a man derives from the fact that he is a member of this house; he has the privilege of speaking in millions. I do not know whether other hon. members are like myself in this regard, but I frankly confess that if I began to talk in such stupendous sums I should not really know what I was talking about. But the fact is striking, nevertheless, that last year we sent into the United States something like $3,000,000 a day. One can hardly grasp it. Let me put it in a more tangible, a more realizable form. I live in a small village of 350 or 400 people-a nice little village which is rated at a valuation of about $100,000. Well, we sent to the United States each day in the year that ended March 31, 1930, an amount equal to the total valuation of 30 villages such as mine. That is what we have done, and we sent a goodly number of Canadians to populate them.
During this great period of prosperity between 1921 and 1929 we have been spending our money on immigration to help to build up the United States and to help to make the people there prosperous. We are just as old a country as the United States. Is there any reason, therefore, why we should occupy the northern half of this continent with a population of 10,000,000, while there is a population of 120,000,000 to the south of us? It seems to me that there has been mismanagement in some direction; I do not believe that the proper policy has been followed. I am quite sincere, Mr. Speaker, in my policy of protection. I want to see it tried, and I am perfectly willing, if it is not successful, to perish in the attempt, as the Prime Minister has put it. I have always contended that with proper protection this country would prosper and grow and Canada would become the boom country of the world. That is my firm conviction.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 hope the hon. member who has just concluded will pardon me if I do not follow his argument. The budget, with its proposed amendments, has been before us since June 1. It has been thoroughly discussed in this house and I believe the people of the country understand it fairly well. There is one thing in the budget with which I think we can all agree, something that has struck a responsive chord in the hearts of all people, and that is the extract from the Chronicles of the Pilgrim Fathers:
It wonderfully encourageth men in their duties, when they see the burthen equally borne; but when some withdraw themselves, and
retire to their own particular case, pleasure, or profit, what heart can men have to go on in their business? When men are come together to lift some weighty piece of timber, or vessel, if one stand still and do not lift, shall not the rest be weakened and disheartened?
Those are the sentiments, and that is the spirit which enabled that little band of pioneers to conquer so many hardships. In that spirit they carried on and endured and accomplished much. We have that sentiment in the budget, but you will search in vain for very much evidence of its application in legislation. We find that taxes have been increased. Of course, we all expected that taxes would be increased. We knew it was necessary'. But unfortunately we find that some taxes have been made easier for those best able to pay, while the taxes which the great mass of the people pay have been increased. We had been expecting something different in these times; we had expected something in the nature of a conscription of wealth. We should not have been much surprised if something in the form of a capital levy had been proposed. But nothing of that sort is seen in the budget. The sales tax is increased from 1 to 4 per cent; postage has been increased from 2 to 3 cents; a stamp tax has been put on all cheques, even those below $10; and taxes have been imposed on oranges, tea, rice, raisins, and very many other articles in common use. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) said that there were
142.000	people paying income tax in this country, and he declared that of that number
100.000	would pay less in the future. The burden will be lightened so far as that number are concerned.
Now, in these days when there are so many people out of work, so many people close to the bread line, does it seem fair that the man or woman who holds a steady position with a salary of $300, $400 or $500 per month should be relieved of the necessity of paying something in the way of income tax? And if we look into the situation a little more closely we shall find that while the income tax is reduced on lower incomes, those in the middle brackets who are actively engaged in the business of the country have to pay more. Very' unfairly, I think, 100 or more of those who pay on large incomes find they are saved large sums of money in settling their income tax accounts. If a man had an income of $500,000, he would save at least $41,000 by this new arrangement. Carry it further and you will find that there is a difference in the way the tax is imposed, depending on whether a man earns his income or gets it from investment. A man receiving dividends is re-
The Budget-Mr. Gershaw

lieved of paying taxation on half his income up to $10,000, and the man who works for his money must pay on all. I believe that this is a step in the wrong direction; I think it is a backward step and one which will not make for happiness and contentment among the Canadian people. We in Canada do not want conditions that prevail in Russia, but the British people in this country are alive to these things at the present time, and they will not indefinitely and indifferently submit to what seems to them to be an injustice, under present conditions.	.
Even as a protectionist budget, it seems to me that there are a few things lacking in this one which is before us. The question of agricultural .production has been a big one, and the tariff problem has been before the people for ages. We believe that such articles of agriculture as we possess in abundance and are on an export basis are not helped by a protective tariff. This country with ten millions of people grows sufficient to feed eighty, ninety or one hundred millions. We must export wheat, bacon, cheese, butter, and other articles of that nature, and a tariff does not help those particular products. Those who sold butter at forty to fifty cents a pound before the tariff was increased and must sell it now at twelve or fifteen cents a pound will agree with that statement. There are other articles which are not on an export basis, and I desire to draw the attention of the house to one or two which are not mentioned in the present budget.
We use in Canada about 60,000,000 pounds of wool, and of that amount we produce about 25,000,000 pounds. We must import a great deal of wool, and I remember hearing Conservative members make long speeches deploring the fact that our sheep population was gradually becoming smaller. Very definite promises were made that something would be done for those in the sheep business when the Conservative party came into power. But we find that nothing has been done in this budget. It is true the textile manufacturers have received a protection of from thirty to thirty-five per cent, but I contend that that protection should be contingent upon the manufacturer using a generous quota of Canadian wool in the manufacture of his goods.
Another problem which I would like to bring to the attention of the house is that which confronts the sugar beeit industry. Every man, woman and child in Canada consumes about 92 pounds of sugar per year. The total yearly consumption in Canada is about 900,000,000 pounds, and of that amount the most we have ever produced locally is around 70,000,000 pounds. I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. 
Bennett) is not in his seat because he is familiar with this subject. He promised definitely at the special session of 1930 that this matter would receive his attention. He said that he would not hesitate to do it at that time were it not for the complicated schedules which would have to be prepared. Other countries have at different times done much to encourage the production of sugar beet. For instance, the United States has imposed an import duty of eleven shillings per hundred pounds against sugar entering that country, except from her own colonies such as Porto Rico, Hawaii and the Philippines. Czechoslovakia has placed an import duty of twenty-one shillings per hundred pounds; Poland, 14s. 2d.; France, 8s. 3d.; Germany, 7s. 6d.; Sweden, 5s. 7d.; Belgium, 4s. 9d.; and, as I have said, the United States, 11s. As I read the tariff schedules, the British preferential rate in Canada is about 35 cents and the general rate about SI-47 per hundred pounds on sugar exceeding ninety-eight degrees of polarization. In 1925 this country entered into a trade agreement with the West Indies. They gave us a preference in their markets for flour, apples, cement, beef, lumber, butter, cheese and other products of that kind, and in return we established a steamship service and gave a preference in our markets for cocoa, eocoanuts and cane sugar. This treaty was to last for twelve years from 1925 and could be abrogated on either country giving one year's notice after that time. I have indicated that about 830,000,000 pounds of sugar are imported into Canada to supply our needs, and of that amount I find that 100,000,000 pounds come from the Fiji islands. I have been unable to find out how far west in Canada the West Indies sugar will reach, but I think it is fair to assume that most of the sugar which goes into the western provinces comes from the Fiji islands and other countries which are not part of the empire. We have 43,464 acres under cultivation for sugar beet growing, with an t average production of eight and a half tons, which gives only 364,000 tons. If the government does not wish to increase the price of sugar by imposing a higher tariff on that commodity, a subsidy of say one dollar per ton could be paid which would allow this industry to prosper and give encouragement to those trying to make a living on the irrigated farms of Canada. Granting a subsidy is not a new thing because other countries have taken this action to increase production. England and the Irish Free State have granted generous subsidies to the sugar industry, and in some countries of Europe cartels have been formed to ensure that sugar would sell for a

The Budget-Mr. Gershaw
reasonable price within the country. For instance, between 1924 and 1928 the government of Great Britain assisted the sugar beet industry by giving a subsidy of 19s. 6d., as well as a subsidy of 3s. lid. on molasses. The difference between the excise tax and the duty on imported refined sugar amounted to about 4s. 3d. The government of Great Britain insisted that refiners use locally grown sugar, and the subsidies paid were contingent upon a fair price being paid to those who were producing sugar within the country. In view of the potential greatness of this industry and in view of the relief which is needed to stabilize the farming industry, it seems to me most regrettable that some assistance has not been given at the present time.
One of the great problems which confront us is that of unemployment. We have always a certain number of unemployed, but at present the number is larger than usual. There are many men out of work who would be glad to do any kind of labour. While it is not true that the world owes every man a living, it probably is true that the world owes every man an opportunity to work. I have just one suggestion to make, which I think might temporarily relieve the great unemployment problem, and that is to make the working hours shorter. If you have one hundred men working and twenty-five men idle you can easily see that by shortening the hours of labour from eight to six hours a day you will give an opportunity to all to work. You may say it will increase the burden on industry. True, it will, but we shall have to pay more money in any case. During the last winter the federal, provincial and municipal governments paid out upwards of 870,000,000 for unemployment relief, and if some of this were used to help to shorten the hours of labour and give employment to more men, much benefit would result. Conditions regarding unemployment have become very acute. Stephen Leacock, writing in 1921, said that the productive ability of the average worker had increased forty-fold in 125 years, and we know that in the last few years with the introduction of labour-saving machinery the average productivity of the individual is continuing to increase. In view of the circumstances some definite steps must be taken.
We speak of this as an ordinary period of depression, but who is there who can see much light ahead at present, and who is there who will say that it will gradually pass away unless we definitely study the problem and take steps to relieve the situation? We have large inventories in many lines of production, but when you go into the homes of the
people you can see that lumber is required to improve these homes, that furniture and washing machines, sewing machines, clothing and other ordinary necessities are required. The difficulty is that while on the one hand we have large stacks of material, on the other hand we have those who require that material but have not the purchasing power to procure it.
There is some difference of opinion as to whether the collapse in wheat prices was the cause of the depression, or whether it was just the victim of it, but we do know that the fall in the price of wheat was one of the greatest factors in prolonging the depression. We do know that there is a serious distribution problem to be faced by the people of this country. This problem of distribution requires the -best thought that the age produces, and we should look to the government and ask what is being done to help to solve these problems. The government have initiated and persisted in a policy of high and higher protection. They hope that by shutting out all goods, our local factories will get the home market, and through mass production be able to produce more cheaply and sell more cheaply. But is this working out? In what direction are the signs pointing? We had the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) speaking in the house this afternoon. He speaks from a point of vantage. He has had a wealth of experience. He has lived through cycles of inflation and deflation. He has seen a dozen governments come and go. By virtue of the high position which he has occupied he has been intimately associated with the legislation which has been enacted during all those fifty years, and we were glad and proud to see him stand up in his place to-day. We listen to him when he says that protection will never cure our economic ills.
But other signs are not lacking. Chambers of commerce, yes, and even the League of Nations, have come to the conclusion that high tariff bariers are doing much to check the natural flow of international trade. Even here in Canada some signs are coming into evidence that prices are not kept down when the tariff is increased. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we would be getting our gasoline more cheaply now if we had not a tariff against it. I hold in my hand a list of prices for repairs for machinery, which was sent out by a large manufacturer of farm implements in this country, dated April 7, 1931. Thirty-six of the articles enumerated in this list have been increased in price, and only four have been decreased. Article listed
The Budget-Mr. Gershaw

as 1387 carried an old price of 11.85, and the new price is $4.85. The next article carried an old price of $18, and the new price is $20. The next article carries an old price of 35 cents, and the new price is 45 cents. If we go down the list, we will find that prices are increased in almost every ease. In fact if you bought one of each of the articles listed here it would cost at the old prioe $84.41, and at the new price $98,56, an increase of 20 per cent in the cost of the producer who requires these machinery repairs.
We see difficulties in other directions as well. It has been stated by the Labour Gazette that the price of raw material between January, 1930, and January, 1931, decreased 32 per cent and wholesale prices 15 per cent. We know that field products have come down by 60 per cent, prime beef by 40 per cent, select pork by 43 per cent, while the cost of living has come down, roughly, only 6 per cent. The farmer finds that the price of the article he has to sell has been greatly reduced, and the price of the article he has to buy has hardly reduced at all, and so he is put in a position in which it is quite impossible for him to pay his ordinary debts.
In conclusion, we find that we have elevators bulging with grain, and warehouses in which the shelves are piled high with wearing apparel and food. We have vast unused hoards of capital, and yet in the world at large we have sixty million of people unemployed. I do not know how great the restlessness and dissatisfaction is throughout Canada. I do know that it will be worse during the coming year, and facing these problems we can easily understand why people see inadequacy in our social system to meet human needs. We do not approve of collectivism or communism or bolshevism, or other forms of chaos and disaster, but we know that there are a great many people who are thinking in that direction, and we know that the best way to meet the menace is to introduce and make good some sound alternative. During the great war the rich as well as the poor were willing to make sacrifices for the country. The rich and those in a position to help are not now any less patriotic than they were at that time, and I believe they would not falter if they were asked to share a greater burden to-day. We find, however, that the government has been standing pat to the old system, by introducing a budget that is perhaps more retrograde and reactionary than ever because it pursues the old line of protection, which is being questioned in so many places. I believe that we

have a right to expect something different, from the government. Armed with their recent verdict from the people the government should present a policy which will give equal opportunities to all and work towards harmony and unity among the Canadian people, a policy which will not tend to widen the breach between one class and another. The government has a clear majority of 29 over all, and I believe it should head right into the storm and demonstrate its courage by some policy which will hold out a hope of solving the problems which face them, a policy which will bring about a greater measure of peace, happiness and contentment among the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a new member of the house I should like to have been able to address the house in the language of the majority of its members. As this is the first occasion, however, upon which I have spoken, I think it is my duty to speak in the langugage with which I am most familiar.
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, before broaching the subject matter of this debate, allow me in my turn to congratulate you on the exalted post you occupy in this house. The dignity and great deference with which you acquit yourself of important functions makes it an agreeable task for me to state that you are worthy of our highest consideration.
I also wish to equally congratulate you on the willingness shown in reading the documents of the house and the prayers in French. I must acknowledge that I was deeply moved by this act of deference on your part. We pray with more fervor and we believe ourselves in closer touch with Divine Providence when we pray in our mother tongue.
May I, sir, offer my thanks to my constituents of Vaudireuil-Soulanges for the mark of confidence reposed in me and which affords me the opportunity, to-day, of taking part in the debates of the house. Realizing my responsibilities towards them, I shall be guided by their interests in all my actions as representative of the people. In the last Parliament the constituency of Vaudreuil-Soulanges was represented by a man whose memory, to his own county, is imperishable. No one in need, in the county, was ever left without help, orphans were specially the object of his zeal; the educational institutions both of his county and the diocese of Valleyfield were the recipients of subscriptions which contributed considerably to enlarging their respective establishments and giving an educa-

The Budget-Mr. Thauvette
tion on easy terms to a greater number of young men, sons of workers or farmers.
I shall not add more for fear of wounding his averseness to publicity. On behalf of his fellow-citizens-my constituents of to-day-I offer my best wishes of better health, longevity and happiness among his own people to the Hon. Lawrence Wilson, a former member of the house, and now the representative of the division of Rigaud in the Senate. Yes, a long life and happiness among his own people so that he may carry on his good work so noteworthy and appreciated in these times of general distress. It is well to remind all those on whom fortune smiles of the lofty deeds of this great philantropist, this eminent financier, who remembers his humble beginning and lavishes part of his wealth on the people with whom he has mingled, and this for the common cause. What a fine achievement sir, when it is done at a time when the people seem to harbour in their souls feelings which, grouped together, are known under various names, but which may give rise to anxious moments for those who are in a position to help, yet do not follow the example of my predecessor in this house.
Allow me now, sir, to refer to other matters. By virtue of the privilege which the rules of the house confer upon me, I deem it my duty to express the feelings of regret and deception which are manifested by the citizens of Canada, especially those who are on the farm. I still recall the charges made by the Conservative candidate, my opponent, against the King government which he stated was responsible for the depression felt in Canada. Tears were in his eyes when he told the farmers of my county that the cause of all their trouble was the New Zealand treaty. He announced the coming of a famous doctor who held the secret of a panacea to all their ills. He contended that with a dose of this serum, unemployment would vanish in three days; that factories would spring up all over Canada; that agriculture would find new markets abroad, because this remedy possessed sufficient explosive power to blast an avenue through which would flow all the surplus of farm products, especially the western wheat. What was the result of this policy from July last to this day? Let us study this policy and its results with reference to the interests of the farming class-that part which interests almost all my constituents. From the very first day of the session-supposed to be an emergency one-in September last, we recognized the dangers of this policy of protection and its prejudicial results to the farming class. I was somewhat disappointed at the various changes which the government made
to the tariff at that session, without giving the house the opportunity of seriously studying the effects of these changes. For instance, out of 28 items referring to agriculture, 14 only are of a nature to benefit the farming class.
It is inconceivable that the present government has not better understood the sad plight in which are placed the farmers. It is nevertheless the labouring class which is most vulnerable to the uncertainty of success, exposed as they are to the sudden changes of weather, over which they have no control. I have listened to numerous speeches from both sides of the house, and I am sorry to say that all agree that agriculture is threatened at its very foundation. I am especially grieved at this unfortunate state of things, because I live among those toilers of the land and I know their joys and sorrows. I have heard the sad complaints of the western farmers. It seems to me, however, that our people are as much to be pitied. It is true that farming in the west is carried out on a larger scale, the farms are vast, while with us their areas are but 60 to 80 acres, and, generally, have been handed down from generation to generation and have become, so to speak, an inheritance which must be kept up at all cost. Alienation is considered almost equivalent to a sacrilege; it is therefore pitiful to hear the crier, on Sunday after mass, in our old Canadian villages, announce to the local people the stipulations governing the public sale of a farm and its equipment Within the last few months these public sale notices have increased to an alarming degree.
The reason for these mishaps and farm desertions, sir, can be traced to the negligence of the present government in not giving sufficient encouragement and hope to the farming class. Quite the opposite, the first act of the government, at the special session in September, resulted in increasing the amount of capital required to operate the farms, by levying duties of 25 to 35 per cent on farm implements, when the sale price of their products had decreased from 50 to 100 per cent. I could quote a number of magazines and newspapers which have collected statistics establishing the truth of this statement.
I shall, however, compare the prices of certain agricultural products in my county for the years 1929 and 1930, they are the retail prices.
In December, 1929, butter sold at 40 cents per pound; in December, 1930, 30 cents. Oats, sold at 1 to H cents per pound in 1929; they sold for J of a cent in 1930. Potatoes sold at $1.25 per bag in 1929; in 1930, the

price was 75 cents. Yet the New Zealand treaty had been abolished in December, 1930, and the King government was no longer in power. Hay is sold at present $7 to $9 per ton in my county, and there is hardly no market for it. Do you suppose that it is encouraging for the farmer to raise hay when he is obliged to pay $3 for the pressing and transport of a ton of hay to the nearest railway station, when he receives but $7 to $9 per ton. This is the exact situation of the farmer and I think that it is the same in almost all counties of our province.
We quite realized, sir, that a Tory government was at the helm of the affairs of this country when we listened to the budget speech for the year 1931-32, by the right hon. Minister of Finance. This statement of increased taxation on almost all articles which are necessary to sustain life, especially among the working and farming classes confirm our fears.
I recall the request made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the right hon. Prime Minister, at the short session, known as an emergency session, last autumn, in which he asked him not to adopt tariff changes without allowing us sufficient time to duly consider them; the Prime Minister promised at the time that these tariff changes would be discussed at the first regular session. However, I have searched through all the speech of the Minister of Finance on the budget and nowhere do I find a single tariff item which was changed at the September session. What has become of the Prime Minister's promise? It has had the fate of all the others.
In going over the list of the tariff items Which were changed last autumn, I note that they all favour the manufacturers and that an increased duty on farm implements was not forgotten. As a result of this protection, farm implements have not been made any cheaper while the prices of all farm products have dropped 100 per cent since then. Let me quote a few examples as regards dairy products. The following prices were obtained by one of my fellow-citizens, a farmer of Vaudreuil who deals with the milk distributors of Montreal: 3,112 pounds of milk sold in December, 1920, to J. J. Joubert & Co. of Montreal brought in a net profit to this farmer of $102.88. In December, 1930, when Mr. Bennett was in office and the New Zealand treaty had passed out of existence, 3,890 pounds of milk brought in $91.74. In May, 1931, 5,204 pounds of milk gave a return of $66.31. And this milk was sold to distributors. However, most of my fellow-citizens 
are unable to bring their milk to Montreal, and they must sell it to the butter factories. This milk, at present, sells in my county for 4 cents a gallon or 40 cents per 100 pounds. This means, that a farmer wishing to send a letter by mail, enclosing his cheque to pay his taxes, at the rate proposed in the budget, would have to sell two gallons of milk in order to despatch that letter.
Eggs sold in January and February from 23 to 25 cents per dozen, that is for strictly fresh eggs, classified as No. 1. They sell at present 15 cents per dozen.
Potatoes retail at 50 to 60 cents per bag. As to this farm product, it would be quite in order to give the house some particulars in respect to the effect of the high tariff adopted by the government. Our best market for the sale of our potatoes is the United States which bought from Canada, during the years 192829 and 1930, for an amount of $11,291,723. While the potato purchases for the whole of Canada amounted to $18,464,584. However, we also import potatoes from the United States. For the years 1928, 1929 and 1930, we imported $2,685,587 worth of potatoes; the balance in our favour being in the ratio of 4 to 1. The regular tariff is 75 cents per 100 pounds; the United States tariff is the same as ours.
A barrel of potatoes sells in the United States $5.70 and contains 3 bushels or 180 pounds. The usual duty would be $1.35 per barrel. The Bennett government for tariff purposes, fixes the price of potatoes imported from the United States at six cents per pound and informs the Canadian importer that he must pay that price to the American exporter, or pay the difference between six cents per pound the value fixed by the government and the market price, by means of an additional duty at the port of entry.
The situation is as follows:
1.	The net price of potatoes is $5.70 per barrel of 180 pounds.
2.	The regular duty is $1.35.
3.	The government fixes the value of a barrel of potatoes for tariff purposes at $10.80.
4.	A special duty is levied on the difference between the market price of $5.70 and the fixed price of $10.80, which means a difference of $5.10.
5.	Adding this special duty of $5.10 to the regular duty of $1.35 we have a duty of $6.45 or 113 per cent of the market price, which simply means that the duty on a barrel of potatoes amounts to $6.45 while previously they were $1.35. Under these conditions a barrel of potatoes would cost $12.15, .previously it cost $7.05. The tariff schedule on this
